In Christ they received the true circumcision “made without hands” — the whole old self cut away in his death; they were buried with him in baptism and raised with him through faith in the mighty working of the God who raised Jesus from the dead. The Christian does not begin with Christ and then climb beyond him; he has already died, been buried, and been raised in union with his Lord. There is no higher to go.

The section reaches its height at the cross. Once dead in trespasses and shut out as unclean outsiders, the Colossians were “made alive together with him” by sheer resurrecting grace — for you do not improve a corpse, you raise it — and forgiven all their trespasses, every last one. The certificate of debt that stood against us, with all its legal demands, God wiped clean and “set aside, nailing it to the cross” — the record of our guilt fastened to Calvary in the flesh of the crucified Son, carried into the grave, and left there paid in full. And in the same stroke the powers the false teachers wanted the church to dread were stripped, shamed, and led away in chains: the cross that looked like Christ’s defeat was his triumphal procession, the principalities of darkness marched behind him as conquered prisoners. So the believer stands both complete and safe in Christ — nothing left to add, and no power left to fear. Everything the false teachers offer as a supplement has already been given, because nothing less than everything has been given in him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Colossians 2:13–15 contains two of the most vivid metaphors for the atonement in the New Testament. First, the legal metaphor: the “record of debt” (cheirographon) that stood against us — the written bond of indebtedness, the document that recorded every sin and violation — has been cancelled, taken out of the way, nailed to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed. Second, the military metaphor: the rulers and authorities who held humanity in their power through guilt and the law’s accusation have been “disarmed” and put to open shame — led in a triumphal procession like conquered enemies behind the victorious general. These two images together show what the cross accomplished: liberation from guilt (the debt cancelled) and liberation from spiritual bondage (the powers defeated).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy appealed to the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as real and threatening forces that needed to be placated through ritual observance. Paul says: those powers have been disarmed. They are defeated enemies, paraded in public shame behind the triumphing Christ. You do not placate them; you stand on the victory that has already been won. Now: The Christian who lives in fear of spiritual powers — who approaches life with anxiety about demonic influence, spiritual attack, or cosmic forces working against them — needs to hear this: the powers have been disarmed. Christ has triumphed. The fear of powers that have been publicly defeated is not piety; it is a failure to reckon with the victory of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names the danger. In v. 4 he warned in general terms that someone might “delude” them; now he sounds the alarm and points straight at the enemy. “See to it” (blepete) is a sharp watchman’s cry — Look out! Beware! — and Paul names the weapons by which the capture is attempted: philosophy, empty deceit, human tradition, the elemental spirits. The threat is no longer a vague shadow; it has a method and a face, and Paul wants the church staring right at it.

“Takes you captive” — and why so few notice when it happens. The word (sylagōgōn) means to carry someone off as plunder — the picture is a slave-raider or a soldier dragging away prisoners of war in chains. The believer is the spoil; the false teacher is the kidnapper. Now here is the thing worth pondering. If a man tried to seize Old Joe physically — to clap him in irons and march him off down the street — everyone would see it at once. People would shout, resist, and call for help; the victim himself would fight and run. But when the kidnapping happens in the realm of ideas — when a teaching quietly carries off a person’s mind and heart into bondage — almost no one notices, least of all the captive. He does not feel like a prisoner; he feels enlightened. He thinks he is going “deeper,” growing wiser, being let in on something grand — while in truth he is being led away in chains. That is what makes false teaching so deadly: spiritual captivity wears the disguise of progress, and the captured mind often imagines itself freer than ever. This is precisely why Paul does not whisper but shouts — Watch out! — because this kidnapping does not look like kidnapping.

The weapons of capture — what each term means. Paul lists four, and they overlap and reinforce one another.

“Philosophy” (philosophia, literally “love of wisdom”). Paul is not condemning all careful thinking — he himself reasoned with the philosophers at Athens. The words that follow define which philosophy he means: this particular system, the Colossian teachers’ speculation that paraded as profound wisdom but was hollow at the core. It had an impressive name and no substance.

“Empty deceit” (kenēs apatēs). Here is the true verdict on that “philosophy”: it is empty — it promises fullness and delivers a void; it dazzles but cannot give what it offers. And it is deceit — it does not merely fail, it misleads. Mark the irony: it leaves a man empty, while in Christ “you have been filled” (v. 10).

“According to human tradition” (paradosin tōn anthrōpōn). Trace its pedigree and you find it comes from men, not from God — handed down by human authority, not given by divine revelation. It is exactly what Jesus charged the Pharisees with: “you leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men” (Mark 7:8). However ancient or respected, its source is merely human.

“According to the elemental spirits of the world” (stoicheia tou kosmou). This phrase is debated. The word can mean the “ABCs,” the elementary first principles — but in Colossians, where angels are venerated and holy days are kept, Paul most likely means the elemental spiritual powers thought to govern the world: the cosmic forces behind the calendar, the stars, and the old order, which men felt they had to appease. They belong to “the world” — the old, fallen, enslaved system — and to crawl back under them is to return to the very slavery Christ broke (cf. Gal. 4:3, 9; these are the same powers Christ “disarmed” at the cross, v. 15).

“And not according to Christ” — the one test that matters. These four words are the hinge of the verse, for they expose the single fatal flaw running through all the rest. The teaching is according to philosophy, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits — but not according to Christ. Christ is the standard, the measuring rod against which every idea is laid. And this is wonderfully freeing for Old Joe. He does not need to become an expert in every cult, master every false system, or study every lie ever told in order to be safe. He needs to know one thing surpassingly well: Christ. Think of how a bank teller is trained to spot forged notes — not by memorizing every counterfeit ever printed, but by handling the genuine bill so constantly that anything false feels wrong the instant it touches his hand. So with the believer. Know Christ deeply — his supremacy, his sufficiency, his finished work — and when a teaching comes that diminishes him, adds to him, or sidelines him, you will feel the wrongness of it at once, however clever it sounds. The question is never merely “is this argument hard to answer?” but “is this according to Christ?” If it is not, it is to be refused, full stop. cf. 1 John 4:1; Gal. 1:8.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For in him” — the ground of everything Paul has just said. The little word “for” tells us this verse is the reason behind the warning of v. 8. Why must the Colossians refuse to be taken captive by philosophy, human tradition, and the elemental spirits, and cling instead to Christ? Because — for — in him dwells the whole fullness of deity. That is the death-blow to every “Christ-plus” scheme: there is nothing to add to Christ, because all of God is already in him. And mark the stress — “in him”: in Christ, and nowhere else. Not in the angels, not in the spiritual powers, not in the impressive philosophy — the entire fullness of God is located in one place, the person of Jesus.

“The whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” — weigh every word. Paul has said something like this before (1:19), but here he sharpens it to its finest point. “The whole fullness” (pan to plērōma) — all of it, the totality, nothing left over and nothing residing elsewhere. “Of deity” (theotētos) — this is the strongest word available. It does not mean merely god-like qualities or a divine sparkle; it means Godhood itself, the very being and essence of God. Christ is not a creature filled up with divine attributes; the complete divine nature — everything it is to be God — resides in him. “Dwells” (katoikei) stands in the present tense and means to settle down and take up permanent residence: not a passing visit, but God at home in Christ, continually, even now in his exalted state. And then the word that crowns it: “bodily” (sōmatikōs) — in bodily form, in a real human body. Here is the incarnation at full stretch: the infinite, undivided fullness of God dwells in the man Christ Jesus, flesh and all — in the body that was born, crucified, and raised. Not that the body shrinks God down or contains him like a jar; rather, in the embodied, incarnate Christ the whole Godhead truly resides. All of God, in a body you could have stood beside.

Why does Paul bring this up here? Because it is the foundation of his entire case against the false teachers, and it strikes them from several sides at once. Against their angels and elemental spirits: if all the fullness of deity is in Christ, those powers have no fullness to offer — why seek lesser mediators when the whole God is yours in Jesus? Against their scattered “fullness”: they pictured the divine fullness as spread thin across a chain of spiritual beings, reached by stages; Paul says it is concentrated, entire and undivided, in Christ alone. Against their contempt for the body: that one word “bodily” rebukes every teaching that despises the physical and seeks God by escaping it — for God himself dwells bodily in Christ; the road to God is not a flight from the material into mystical thin air, but the embodied Lord Jesus. And it lays the ground for the very next line (v. 10): because the fullness lives in Christ, and you live in Christ, you have been filled — you lack nothing. To go hunting for “more” beyond him is to turn your back on the fullness of God to chase empty shadows. For Old Joe the comfort is total: he does not hold a fragment of God or a junior deputy; in Christ he has all of God there is to have. cf. Col. 1:19; John 1:14; 14:9.

verseByVerse.quote: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And” — the breathtaking conclusion. The little word “and” carries us straight from Christ to ourselves. Verse 9 said the whole fullness of deity dwells in him; verse 10 draws the staggering inference — and you have been filled in him. Notice the deliberate word-link Paul builds: the fullness (plērōma) dwells in Christ, and you have been filled (peplērōmenoi) in Christ — the same root. What is true of the Head overflows to the members. Because the fullness is in him, and you are in him, his fullness becomes yours.

“You have been filled in him.” Three things sit in this short phrase. First, the tense: “have been filled” is a Greek perfect — a completed action with lasting results. It does not say you are slowly being filled, or that you might one day be filled if you climb high enough; it says you have been filled and you remain full. It is done. Second, it is passive: God filled you; you did not fill yourself. And third, “in him” — this fullness is yours not by your own attainment but by your union with Christ; outside him you are empty, in him you are complete. Here is the hammer-blow to the heresy. The false teachers told the Colossians they were lacking — that they needed more rituals, more knowledge, more experiences to reach fullness. Paul answers flatly: you are already full in Christ. How can anyone add to fullness? (This does not mean Old Joe is sinlessly perfect or personally possesses deity; it means he lacks nothing for salvation, nothing for access to God, nothing for true spiritual completeness — it is all his in Christ.)

“Who is the head of all rule and authority.” Paul calls Christ the head — the source and the sovereign — over “all rule and authority.” Those words name the spiritual powers, the angelic and cosmic beings: the very “rulers and authorities” the false teachers urged the church to revere and appease. But Paul has already said Christ created them (1:16) and will soon say he disarmed them at the cross (2:15); here he says he is their head. Every rank of power that exists, friendly or hostile, stands beneath him. He is at once the head of the body, the church (1:18), and the head of the whole unseen realm of powers — supreme over both. So the beings the Colossians were tempted to fear and flatter are themselves subjects of the One they already belong to.

Why does Paul press this, and what does it mean for Old Joe? Two great comforts, each aimed straight at the heresy. First, you are complete. Old Joe may quietly feel like a second-rate Christian — sure that the “real” believers have deeper experiences, secret knowledge, or special blessings he is missing. Paul tells him plainly: in Christ you have been filled. You are not lacking. You need not chase the next experience or technique to “arrive” — you have already arrived in Christ. It is like a man with a fortune already in his account fretting that he is poor; the answer is not to earn more but to wake up to what is already his and start drawing on it. Second, you stand over the powers, not under them. The Colossians lived in dread of the spiritual realm — angels to appease, cosmic forces to obey. Old Joe has his own version: a vague fear of fate, of dark forces, of the unseen, of whatever might be pulling the strings behind life. Paul’s answer is the same: the One you belong to is the head over every power that exists. They all answer to him; not one of them outranks your Lord. So the believer does not cower before the unseen world or bargain with it — he is joined to its King. There is nothing left to fear, and nothing left to add. cf. Eph. 1:21–22; Rom. 8:38–39.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Circumcised with a circumcision made without hands” — what is Paul teaching? The false teachers were pressing the old physical rite of circumcision and the rules that came with it. Paul cuts the ground from under them: in Christ you have already received the true circumcision — not one “made with hands” by a human knife, but one “made without hands,” worked by God himself. And what is cut away is not a small piece of flesh but “the body of the flesh” — the whole old sinful self, the life ruled by sin. This was always what circumcision pointed to: even in the Old Testament the real thing was the “circumcision of the heart” (Deut. 30:6; Jer. 4:4; Rom. 2:28–29) — a heart cleansed and set apart for God. Paul calls it “the circumcision of Christ,” pointing to Christ’s own death, his being “cut off,” in which the believer shares. At the cross the old self was decisively cut away; united to Christ’s death, you received the only circumcision that finally matters. The Judaizer’s knife can add nothing to it.

“Having been buried with him in baptism” — what does that mean? Baptism pictures, and seals, the believer’s union with Christ. To go down into the water is to be buried with him — the old life is not merely improved but put in the grave alongside Christ’s buried body (cf. Rom. 6:3–4). Notice how Paul sets circumcision (v. 11) and baptism (v. 12) side by side as signs of one and the same reality: the cutting away and burial of the old self in union with Christ. The point is not the rite itself but what the rite proclaims — that in Christ you have died and been buried; that chapter of you is closed.

“In which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God.” Baptism does not stop at the grave. As the believer comes up out of the water, it portrays the next thing: raised with him. Union with Christ is union with his resurrection as well as his death — the old self buried, and a new self raised to new life (the very thing Paul will build on in 3:1, “if then you have been raised with Christ”). And mark how this happens: “through faith in the powerful working of God.” It is not the water that raises anyone, not the ritual operating by itself; it is the mighty power (energeia) of God, laid hold of by faith. Faith is the empty hand that receives; God’s power is what actually raises. So no one is swept into new life mechanically by a ceremony — the resurrection-life comes to those who trust the God who works it.

“Who raised him from the dead” — and notice who does the raising. Here Paul says God (the Father) raised Jesus from the dead. Yet elsewhere Scripture says the Spirit raised him (“the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead,” Rom. 8:11), and elsewhere still the Son raised himself (“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”; “I have authority to lay down my life, and authority to take it up again,” John 2:19; 10:18). This is no muddle and no contradiction. It is a window into the Trinity: the resurrection is the one, undivided act of the one God, who is Father, Son, and Spirit. Each Person is fully God, and all three are at work in the works of God. There is no rivalry in the Godhead, only the seamless cooperation of the three Persons in a single mighty deed. And here is the comfort folded into it: the greatest display of power in all history — the full might of the triune God raising Jesus — is the very power that raised you with him, and that is at work in you now. cf. Eph. 1:19–20.

What is the point of all this — and why does Paul bring it up here? Old Joe may well be puzzled: in the middle of warning against false teachers, why pile up circumcision, burial, baptism, and resurrection? Here is the thread. The false teachers were saying, “You need more — be circumcised, keep our rules, climb higher to reach completeness.” Paul’s reply is to show what has already happened to the believer in Christ. You have already received the true circumcision — the old self cut away by God. You have already died and been buried with Christ — that chapter is closed. You have already been raised with him to new life by the same power that raised Jesus from the grave. What, then, could anyone possibly add? You cannot improve on death and resurrection. This is the deep ground of “you have been filled in him” (v. 10): you are complete because you have been so totally joined to Christ that everything he did has become yours. When Old Joe trusted Christ he did not merely sign up for a religion or bolt Jesus onto his old life; he was so united to the Saviour that what happened to Christ happened to him — Christ’s death became his death, Christ’s resurrection his resurrection. The rites the heretics were peddling are only shadows of a reality Old Joe already possesses in full. So he need not feel half-finished or second-rate; he is a man who has been through the grave and out the other side in Christ — and he is now to live as the raised man he already is. cf. Rom. 6:4–5; Col. 3:1–4.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh” — how bad was our condition? Paul does not say we were sick, or weak, or struggling. He says we were dead. Before God’s grace reached us we were spiritual corpses — unable to respond to God, unable to raise ourselves, unable to contribute one thing to our own rescue (the same verdict as Eph. 2:1). And Paul names two layers of the ruin. “In your trespasses” — sin was the killer; our false steps and rebellions were the very thing we lay dead in. “The uncircumcision of your flesh” — the Colossians were Gentiles, physically uncircumcised, outside the covenant people of God (“the uncircumcision,” Eph. 2:11–12); and deeper still, “uncircumcision of the flesh” pictures the unrenewed, uncleansed heart, the old self with nothing yet cut away. So we were doubly lost: dead in guilt, and shut out as strangers, with hearts unclean. That is the pit Paul is about to show us being lifted out of.

“God made alive together with him” — what this means, and what it does not. Into that grave God speaks life. “Made alive together with” (one word in Greek, synezōopoiēsen) is resurrection language — God did for us exactly what he did for Christ in the tomb. Notice what this means: that the new life is entirely God’s doing, and entirely bound up with Christ — we live because he lives, raised together with him. Now notice what it does not mean. It does not mean we were partly alive and God merely topped us up; the dead do not help raise themselves. It does not mean self-improvement, turning over a new leaf, a better effort — you do not improve a corpse, you raise it. And it does not mean we earned this by a decision or a work, for God made us alive while we were still dead (Eph. 2:5) — and a dead man brings nothing to his own resurrection but the deadness from which he is raised. This is grace at its purest and most powerful: not God helping those who help themselves, but God giving life to those who had none. cf. John 5:21; Eph. 2:4–5.

“Having forgiven us all our trespasses” — all of them. The word for “forgiven” (charisamenos) is built on the word for grace: forgiveness is a free gift, graciously given, never earned. And then comes the word to stop the heart: all. Not some. Not the small ones. Not only the sins committed up to the day you believed. All your trespasses — past, present, and future; great and small; the ones you remember and the thousand you have forgotten; the secret ones no living soul knows, and the scarlet ones that make you wince in the dark. Every single one, forgiven. God did not pardon most of your sins and keep a private reserve of charges against you; he did not wipe the slate half-clean. He forgave all. There is no sin of Old Joe’s lying outside this word — not the one that haunts him at three in the morning, not the one he has never confessed to another living soul, not the besetting sin he keeps stumbling back into. All of it, gone. And this is no cheap amnesty, no looking the other way; it is possible only because Christ bore every one of those sins himself — the completeness of the pardon rests on the completeness of his payment, which the next words make vivid. cf. Ps. 103:12; Mic. 7:19; 1 John 1:9.

“Canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands” — the picture explained. Yes, this is a figure of speech, and a vivid one. The “record of debt” translates a single Greek word, cheirographon — literally a “hand-written document,” the ordinary legal term for a certificate of debt: an IOU, a promissory note, written and signed by the debtor himself, acknowledging exactly what he owed. Picture God keeping a ledger of all we owe him — every commandment broken, every obligation of obedience left unpaid — an itemized account “with its legal demands,” the law’s righteous requirements standing in writing against us. That signed bond of guilt was the thing that condemned us; it had our name on it, and the figures were beyond all paying. And what did God do with it? He “canceled” it — the word (exaleiphō) means to wipe out, to erase, to wash the ink clean off the page. Not deferred, not reduced, not suspended — erased, as though the debt had never been written. cf. Isa. 43:25.

“This he set aside, nailing it to the cross” — and here the wonder breaks open. God “set it aside” — took the whole condemning document out of the way — by nailing it to the cross. There is a deliberate, staggering picture here. When the Romans crucified a man, they nailed his charge-sheet (the titulus) to the cross above his head, listing the crime he was dying for; above Jesus it read, “King of the Jews” (John 19:19). But Paul says it was our certificate of debt that was nailed up at Calvary. Now press the question the picture itself raises: it was Jesus who was nailed to that cross — so in what way was our record of debt nailed there? Because our debt was laid on him. The document of our guilt did not drift to the cross on its own; it was fastened there in the flesh of the Son of God, who took our debt as his own and carried it into death. When the nails were driven through his hands, the bond that stood against us was driven through with them. He bore the charge-sheet that had Old Joe’s name on it, signed it over to himself, and took it down into the grave — and it never came back out. The debt is not outstanding somewhere, waiting to resurface; it is buried in the tomb of Jesus, and the empty tomb is the receipt stamped “paid in full.” Every charge against you was answered in the body of Christ. cf. Isa. 53:5–6; Gal. 3:13; 1 Pet. 2:24.

verseByVerse.quote: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The rulers and authorities” — who were they? Not human kings and governors, but the spiritual powers — the fallen angelic and demonic beings, the “cosmic powers over this present darkness…the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). These are the same “rulers and authorities” Paul has already named: created by Christ (1:16), ruled by Christ as their head (2:10), and — crucially for Colossae — the very powers the false teachers were urging the church to revere, fear, and appease (the “worship of angels,” 2:18). They are real, personal, malevolent beings, not mere metaphors and not impersonal forces. And they held humanity in a threefold grip: as the powers behind our sin, as accusers wielding the law’s condemnation against us (the very debt-record of v. 14), and through the fear of death (Heb. 2:14–15). The Colossians lived under their shadow. Paul is about to announce that the shadow has been broken.

“He disarmed” them — how, and why? The word (apekdysamenos) means to strip off, as a soldier is stripped of his armour and weapons. What was the powers’ great weapon against us? Not brute force, but our sin and its just condemnation. The devil is “the accuser” (Rev. 12:10); his whole case against us rested on the unpaid debt of our guilt and the law’s righteous sentence — and behind it, the power of death. Now see how this verse is welded to the last one. In v. 14 God cancelled the debt and nailed it to the cross; in v. 15 he disarms the powers — because the debt was their weapon. Once the record of guilt is wiped out and sin is fully paid for, the accuser has nothing left to accuse with; the jailer has lost his keys; death has lost its sting (1 Cor. 15:55–56). At the cross the weapon was wrenched clean out of their hands. And here is the deep irony: at Calvary it looked as though the powers had won — they “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8) — but in that very act they were destroyed. The cross, their apparent triumph, was their undoing.

“Put them to open shame” — how, and before whom? The phrase (edeigmatisen en parrēsia) means to make a public example of someone, to expose them openly and boldly. Once these powers wore an air of terrifying prestige; now they are publicly disgraced, held up as a spectacle of defeat. Before whom? Before the whole watching unseen world — the cosmos of angels and powers in the heavenly places, who now see their would-be masters exposed as beaten. (Through the gospel and the church this open verdict is published wider still; Eph. 3:10.) The humiliation is as public as their pretended dominion was proud. And that calls up one unmistakable picture, which Paul now names outright.

“By triumphing over them in him” — the Roman triumph. The word (thriambeusas) is the technical term for a triumph — the highest honour Rome could bestow on a victorious general. He would parade into the city in a chariot at the head of his army, his plunder carried before him, and his conquered enemy kings dragged in chains behind him, stripped and humiliated, displayed to the jeering crowds before being led off to execution. Paul casts Christ as that triumphant General, and the rulers and authorities as the captive kings shuffling in chains behind his chariot. The cross, which the watching world saw as Christ’s shameful defeat, was in reality his victory parade — the principalities of hell led behind him as prisoners of war. And “in him” (or “in it,” in the cross) is the crowning irony of history: the very instrument of humiliation and death became the chariot of triumph. The place that looked like the powers’ greatest victory was the stage of their public ruin. cf. 2 Cor. 2:14; Eph. 4:8.

Why does Paul bring this in — and what does it mean for Old Joe? It can feel as though Paul has suddenly changed the subject; he has not. This is the knockout blow of the whole argument. The false teachers were telling the Colossians that they had to fear, navigate, and appease these spiritual powers in order to be safe and to reach God. Paul’s answer is devastating: the cross did not only forgive your sins (v. 14) — it defeated the very powers you are being told to dread. Christ has stripped them, shamed them, and led them in chains. So why would anyone bow to, or bargain with, or tremble before an enemy his own Lord has already conquered and publicly disgraced? You do not flatter a king who is being dragged through the streets in chains; you do not appease a disarmed prisoner. The whole foundation of the heresy collapses. Now, Old Joe may not fear “principalities” by that name, but he has his own dread of the unseen — of evil, of the devil, of dark forces, of whatever might be working against him in the shadows. To him Paul says the same thing: the powers of darkness are a defeated enemy. The devil is real, but he is beaten — disarmed, shamed, and chained behind the cross. He is like a fierce guard dog on a short chain: he still barks and lunges and can frighten the timid, but he is bound, and he cannot drag down the one who belongs to the Victor. Old Joe is not called to fear the spiritual world or to buy it off; he is called to stand in the finished victory of Christ. The decisive battle is already won. cf. James 4:7; Rom. 16:20; 1 John 3:8.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With the great victory of the cross secured, Paul turns it into a charge: since the powers are disarmed, the debt cancelled, and you complete in Christ — let no one sit in judgment on you over food and drink, festivals, new moons, or sabbaths. He does not argue the merits of each rule; he reframes them all. These were “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” A shadow is real and God-given — it traces the shape of what is coming — but once the body that casts it has arrived, to cling to the outline is not deeper piety; it is to turn from the person to his silhouette.

Paul then unmasks the false teacher himself. He would “disqualify” the Colossians, like a crooked umpire robbing them of a prize already theirs, unless they took up his program of self-imposed severity, the veneration of angels, and the parade of visionary experiences. It looks like humility and spiritual depth; in truth the man is “puffed up…by his sensuous mind” — the very flesh he claims to master is what inflates him. And beneath all the display lies the fatal flaw: he is “not holding fast to the Head.” For it is from Christ the Head, and from him alone, that the whole body is nourished, knit together, and grows with a growth that is from God. Cut off from the Head there is no life and no growth — only an impressive death.

Finally Paul lays the axe to the root of rule-religion. Since you died with Christ to the elemental principles of the world, why live as though you still belonged to it, submitting again to “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch”? Such rules fuss over perishable things, rest on merely human commands, and — for all their impressive “appearance of wisdom” in self-made religion, asceticism, and severity to the body — are powerless to do the one thing they promise. They cannot curb the flesh; they only relocate it, feeding pride while starving the body. What austerity could never accomplish, union with the crucified and risen Christ already has. And that sets up the great turn of chapter 3: the answer to a dead religion of rules is not less effort but a new direction — upward, to the risen Christ, where the believer’s true life now is.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance: The Old Covenant as Anticipation

Paul’s description of the Mosaic observances as “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (v. 17) is the hermeneutical principle underlying all Reformed typological interpretation of the Old Testament. The ceremonial law — the festivals, the sabbaths, the food laws, the sacrificial system — was genuinely given by God and genuinely pointed forward to the reality that was coming. But it was always a shadow, not the substance; always anticipation, not fulfilment. The substance arrived in Christ. To return to the shadow when the substance is present is not faithfulness to the law; it is a failure to read what the law was always saying.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers were using Jewish observances as part of their syncretic system, insisting that the Colossians needed to keep certain days and food laws and festivals. Paul says: these were shadows pointing to Christ; Christ has come. Now: The same principle applies to any Christian movement that makes Old Testament ceremonial practices the standard of Christian spirituality. The principles of justice, love, and holiness that the ceremonial law expressed are fulfilled in Christ and applied by the Spirit. The specific ceremonies have been fulfilled in him who was their substance all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore” — the practical turn. Paul now draws the conclusion from everything he has just said. Because you have been filled in Christ (v. 10), because the record of debt with all its legal demands was cancelled and nailed to the cross (v. 14), because the powers behind the old order have been disarmed (v. 15) — therefore do not let anyone drag you back under a system of religious rules. The argument runs straight from doctrine to duty: since Christ has set the legal demands aside, no one may now bind you with them again. What you are in Christ settles how you stand before these would-be judges.

“Let no one pass judgment on you…food and drink…festival…new moon…Sabbath” — what was going on? The false teachers were pressing the Colossians to keep a body of religious regulations — rules about clean and unclean food and drink, and the observance of sacred days. That last list is telling: “festival…new moon…Sabbath” is the standard Old Testament summary of the Jewish sacred calendar — the yearly feasts, the monthly new-moon celebrations, and the weekly Sabbath (cf. 1 Chron. 23:31; 2 Chron. 31:3; Ezek. 45:17). So the heresy had a strong legalistic streak, drawn from the law of Moses and sharpened with extra ascetic demands. And the teachers were “passing judgment” — condemning the Colossians for not keeping these rules, making them feel second-class, unspiritual, disqualified. Paul forbids it flatly: let no one sit in judgment over you on such matters. Your standing is in Christ, not in menus and calendars.

And there is a reason these things can no longer be made binding, which Paul gives in the next verse: they were “a shadow of the things to come” (v. 17). The food laws and the holy days were signposts pointing forward to Christ — and now that the reality has come, to be forced back onto the shadow is to turn away from the substance. The rest the Sabbath pointed to is found in him (Heb. 4:9–10); the feasts that foreshadowed redemption are fulfilled in his cross. To make these regulations a condition of acceptance with God is, in effect, to deny that Christ is enough. (Paul is not calling such observances sinful — a believer may hold his own convictions about days and food, Rom. 14 — but he will not let them be made the measure of anyone’s standing before God.)

What might these “food and days” be today? The exact rules change; the dynamic never does. It is the same error whenever a secondary or man-made practice is made the measure of true spirituality and people are judged by it. It wears modern clothes: “a real Christian would never touch a drink”; you must follow this diet, this fast, this health regime to be holy; you must keep (or must not keep) Christmas, Easter, or Lent; you must use only this Bible translation, sing only these songs, dress to this code, school your children in this one way, hold your quiet time at this hour. Wherever someone takes a matter that Christ has left free and turns it into a test of whether you are accepted by God or a mature believer — and looks down on you for failing it — that is the Colossian heresy in a Sunday suit. And mark that the rebuke cuts both ways: Old Joe is not to let anyone make him feel like a second-rate Christian over such things, and neither is he to sit in judgment on a brother who differs from him (Rom. 14:1–4). But notice carefully what Paul is — and is not — saying. This is no licence to despise all discipline or to do as one pleases; the gospel never frees us to sin, only from it. It is liberty of conscience: Christ, and Christ alone, is the ground of our acceptance, and no one may add a single rule to him. cf. Gal. 5:1; Rom. 14:17.

verseByVerse.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“A shadow of the things to come” — what does Paul mean? “These” — the food laws and holy days of v. 16 — are “a shadow.” Think of what a shadow is: the dark outline an object throws when the light falls behind it. It has the shape of the thing but none of its substance — you cannot shake a shadow’s hand. The whole ceremonial law was exactly that: a God-given shadow cast ahead of a coming reality. And the reality it traced was Christ. The Passover lamb outlined the Lamb of God; the Day of Atonement outlined his once-for-all sacrifice; the Sabbath outlined the rest he gives; the tabernacle outlined God come to dwell with his people. A shadow is real and useful — it truly tells you something is on its way — but it was never meant to be clung to as though it were the thing itself. cf. Heb. 10:1; Heb. 8:5.

“But the substance belongs to Christ.” The word translated “substance” is literally body (sōma), and the contrast is deliberate and beautiful: the shadow (skia) set over against the body that casts it. A shadow is thrown by a solid body standing in the light — and the body that cast this entire shadow-play, the whole Old Testament system, is Christ himself. He is the reality, the solid thing, the substance every regulation was only sketching in outline. And here is the simple force of it: once the body has arrived, you do not go on clutching at the shadow. When your friend himself walks through the door, you do not keep staring at his silhouette on the wall. To return to the ceremonial rules now that Christ has come is to prefer the outline to the person. So Old Joe has lost nothing by leaving the shadows behind — he has gained the very One they were all pointing to. Every feast, every sabbath, every sacrifice was a finger tracing the shape of Jesus before he came; and now that he has come, the finger has found what it was pointing at. To have Christ is to possess the substance of everything the law foreshadowed. cf. Matt. 5:17; John 5:39.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let no one disqualify you” — what was going on? The word (katabrabeuō) comes from the athletic games: the brabeus was the umpire who awarded the prize, and to katabrabeuō someone is to rule against him, to rob him of his prize, to declare him out of the running. So the false teachers were setting themselves up as umpires over the Colossians’ faith, pronouncing them disqualified — missing out on the real prize, not truly in the race — unless they took up the teachers’ program. It is the same condemning posture as the “passing judgment” of v. 16, now sharpened: a self-appointed spiritual elite telling ordinary believers they had not really arrived. Paul’s reply: do not let anyone rob you of a prize that is already yours in Christ. And what was the program they were pushing? Paul lists its three strands.

“Asceticism” — the first strand. The Greek says, literally, that the false teacher “delights in humility” — but a humility of a twisted kind: a self-imposed severity toward the body. This is asceticism: rigorous fasting, harsh self-denial, going without, treating the body roughly as a path to higher spirituality (Paul names it again in v. 23, “severity to the body”). The idea was that by punishing the flesh one could rise to deeper experiences and gain access to God. It looked humble — even impressive — but it was a performance of lowliness, not the real thing. (This is no attack on genuine self-discipline or fasting, which Scripture commends; it is the turning of bodily severity into a badge of spiritual rank.)

“Worship of angels” — the second strand. The Colossians were being urged to give religious devotion to angelic beings — to venerate them as mediators and guardians of the cosmic order, channels through which one might safely approach God. (Some read the phrase as joining in the worship the angels offer in the heavenly realm, claimed by the visionaries; either way, angels are given a place that belongs to Christ alone.) The error is plain: it dethrones the one Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5) and bows to the very powers that Christ is head over (2:10). Angels themselves will not allow it — when John fell down to worship one, the angel refused: “You must not do that…worship God” (Rev. 19:10).

“Going on in detail about visions” — the third strand. The false teacher paraded “the things he had seen” — mystical visions and supernatural experiences gained through his disciplines (the word behind “going on in” may be a technical term for an initiate “entering” the inner sanctuary). He took his stand on these experiences, dwelt on them, built his authority from them: “I have seen things you have not; I have access to the heavenly realm; follow me, and you can too.” It was spiritual one-upmanship by experience — making private revelations, rather than Christ and his Word, the measure of who is truly advanced.

“Puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind” — Paul’s verdict. Now Paul lances the whole thing. For all its impressive display, the man is simply “puffed up” — swollen, inflated with pride — and “without reason,” groundlessly: there is nothing actually there. And the killing stroke: he is puffed up “by his sensuous mind” — literally, “the mind of his flesh.” Here is the irony at the heart of it. The man who beats his body to escape the flesh, who scales the heavens in visions to rise above it, is in fact being driven the whole time by the flesh — by the fallen nature’s craving for status, recognition, and superiority. The austerity feeds his pride; the visions feed his self-importance; his “humility” is vanity in disguise. It is all about self — animated not by the Spirit of God but by the flesh wearing spiritual dress.

What might these strands be today? All three are still with us. Asceticism reappears wherever holiness is equated with severity — extreme diets or fasts worn as spiritual medals, a grim legalism that measures godliness by how much one denies oneself, the quiet assumption that the harder I am on myself the holier I must be. Angel-veneration resurfaces in the modern fascination with angels, “spirit guides,” and cosmic “energies,” and, within the church, in every tendency to slip other mediators — saints, special “anointed” figures — between the believer and Christ. Visionary one-upmanship lives on in the experience-chasing that rates a Christian by whether he has had dramatic encounters, special revelations, or ecstatic experiences, and in the leader who builds a following on his private visions rather than on Christ and Scripture. Beneath all of them runs the same two-part error Paul named: a spiritual elite making ordinary believers feel disqualified unless they add some extra practice or experience to Christ — and, underneath the impressive show, the same fleshly pride. The safeguard, in every age, is the next verse: hold fast to the Head. cf. 1 Cor. 8:1; Col. 2:23.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Not holding fast to the Head” — what did Paul have in mind? “Holding fast” (krateō) means to grip tightly, to cling, to keep a firm hold. And “the Head” is Christ (as in 1:18 and 2:10). So here, in five words, is Paul’s diagnosis of the entire heresy: for all his visions and disciplines and angel-talk, the false teacher has let go of Christ. He has shifted his grip — from the Saviour to rules, experiences, and spiritual beings. And that is fatal, because everything depends on keeping hold of the Head. It is the exact opposite of the healthy Christian Paul described a few verses back, “rooted and built up in him” (2:7). Note too what the word implies: the believer is called actively to hold on — not to drift, not to loosen his grip when something newer and more impressive comes along. Anything that draws your hand off Christ to grasp something extra is pulling you away from the only One who gives life.

“From whom the whole body…grows” — the metaphor. Christ is the Head; the church is his body. And from the Head — and from nowhere else — the whole body draws its life. Paul fills in the anatomy: the body is “nourished” (supplied, fed) and “knit together” (joined, bound into one) “through its joints and ligaments” — the connecting tissues that both link the parts to one another and carry the supply down from the head to every limb. The picture is of life flowing from Christ the Head, through all the connections, into every member, so that the body is at once fed and held together — and therefore grows. And the growth, Paul says, “is from God”: the increase is God’s own doing, his gift, not something the body manufactures by its own effort or technique (cf. Eph. 4:15–16; 1 Cor. 3:6–7). Real growth comes down from the Head; it is never worked up from below.

So that Old Joe gets it. Here is the whole thing in a picture. Cut a branch from the vine, and it does not grow — it withers and dies, because all the life was in the vine (John 15:5). Sever a hand from the arm, and no amount of exercise will make it grow; it is finished the moment it is cut off. That is exactly what the false teachers were unwittingly doing: by drawing people off Christ onto their rules and visions, they were cutting the branch from the vine — offering a fancier life while severing it from its only source. So two things for Old Joe. First, his spiritual growth is not a technique he must master; it is the natural fruit of staying joined to Jesus. His job is to hold fast to the Head — to keep close to Christ in faith, in the Word, in prayer — and God himself supplies the growth. Stop hunting for life in programs and experiences and rule-keeping; stay gripped to Christ, and you will grow, because the life flows from him. Second, he does not grow alone: he grows as part of the body, knit to other believers, the life of the Head running through the connections. A Christian was never meant to be a severed limb. Hold fast to the Head, stay joined to the body, and leave the growing to God.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations — ‘Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch’…? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world” — what does this mean? The “if” is not a doubt but a settled fact: since you died with Christ. The “elemental spirits” (stoicheia, as in v. 8) are the basic governing principles and powers of the old order — the whole system of religious rules and the spiritual forces behind it, the ABCs of a world running apart from Christ. And Paul says you died to all of it. United to Christ in his death (2:11–12), you were severed from that old regime, released from its jurisdiction — for death dissolves every old bond and obligation (Rom. 7:1–6). The elemental rules have no more claim on you than a master has on a slave who has died.

“As if you were still alive in the world” — but were they not alive? Alive, yes — physically, they were breathing and walking about. But they had died, with Christ, to “the world” in Paul’s sense: the old order organized apart from God, the realm of the elemental rules. So to take up that world’s regulations again is to behave “as if” they still belonged to it — as if the death had never happened, as if they were still under its sway and owed it obedience. Paul calls it submitting to “regulations” (literally, letting yourself be decreed at). It is a freed slave voluntarily walking back into the slave-quarters and picking up his old chains. Why, Paul presses, would a dead-and-risen people live by the rule-book they were freed from?

“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” — the regulations themselves. Paul quotes the slogans of the system, and notice their character: every one is a prohibition — don’t, don’t, don’t. A religion of forbiddings, fussing over contact with certain foods and objects. The rules even pile up pettily — “touch” is lighter than “handle,” so that even the faintest contact is banned. This is the asceticism of v. 18 reduced to its bumper-sticker slogans, and Paul lets their narrowness speak for itself.

“Things that all perish as they are used” — the deflation. In a quiet aside Paul lets the air out of the whole system: the things these rules agonize over — foods and the like — are perishable. They “perish as they are used”: eaten, consumed, passed through the body, and gone. They cannot touch the soul (the Lord said as much — what enters the stomach does not defile the heart, Mark 7:18–19). Why would anyone build his standing before God on rules about things destined for the rubbish heap?

“According to human precepts and teachings” — where the rules come from. Here is the decisive stroke: these regulations are man-made. They are “human precepts and teachings,” not the commands of God — the very phrase the Lord Jesus flung at the Pharisees, quoting Isaiah: “teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Mark 7:7; Isa. 29:13). And that settles their authority over the conscience: none. Rules God never gave cannot bind a soul God has freed.

“An appearance of wisdom” — why they are so attractive. Paul grants it: these things “have indeed an appearance of wisdom.” They look wise — rigorous, profound, deeply spiritual. The fasting looks like serious devotion; the strict rules look like holiness; the severity looks like depth. That is exactly their danger: it is a reputation of wisdom, a convincing surface, with no reality beneath. The most dangerous religion is always the kind that looks most like the real thing.

“Self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body” — what that surface trades on. Three things give the system its impressive look. Self-made religion translates a word Paul coins here and which appears nowhere else in all of Greek — ethelothrēskia, “will-worship”: worship a man chooses for himself, devotion springing from human will rather than from God’s command. Asceticism is the show of “humility” again (as v. 18). And severity to the body (apheidia sōmatos, literally “unsparingness”) is harsh, merciless treatment of the body — punishing the flesh to prove one’s seriousness. Self-chosen worship, paraded humility, bodily rigour: it is a religion that looks magnificent. But Paul’s coined word exposes its root — it is self-will dressed up as devotion, religion invented by man rather than revealed by God.

“Of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” — the verdict that brings it all down. For all the impressive show, the whole system fails at the one thing it claims to do: it cannot actually curb sin. External prohibition does not conquer the flesh; it only relocates it. Starve the body, and the flesh does not die — it grows fat on pride, swelling with self-righteous satisfaction in its own discipline. The man who renounces certain foods to subdue his flesh simply finds his flesh feeding on the conquest. Rules can trim outward behaviour, but they cannot change a heart, and they may even inflame the very sin they forbid (Rom. 7:5–8). The flesh is not defeated by a rule-book; it is defeated only by death and resurrection with Christ — which is exactly where Paul turns next (3:1–5).

The whole passage, for Old Joe. Here is Paul’s point in plain words. You died with Christ to the old world of rule-keeping, so do not crawl back under man-made religious rules as though you still belonged to it. Such rules — don’t handle, don’t taste, don’t touch — look wise and holy and rigorous, and they are dangerously attractive. But three things are wrong with them: they are invented by men, not given by God; they fuss over perishable, material things that cannot touch the soul; and — the fatal flaw — they have no power whatever to make Old Joe holy. They are like cutting weeds off at ground level: the garden looks tidy for a day, but the roots are alive and the weeds come straight back. Only Christ digs out the root. So Old Joe must not measure his walk with God by a list of don’ts, and must not let a strict, impressive, self-denying religion fool him into thinking it can change his heart. The cure for sin is not a tighter rule-book; it is a living Saviour. He has died and been raised with Christ — so the way forward is not to climb back under the rules, but to hold fast to the Head and live the new life from above, which is precisely what chapter 3 will now unfold. cf. Rom. 8:13; Gal. 5:16.

3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the ethical consequence of everything chapters 1–2 have established. The logic is characteristically Pauline: because of who you are in Christ (indicative), live accordingly (imperative). You have died with Christ; you have been raised with Christ; your life is hidden with Christ in God; Christ is your life. Therefore: set your minds on things above, put to death what is earthly in you, put off the old self, put on the new self — and let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, the word of Christ dwell in you richly, and everything you do be done in the name of the Lord Jesus.

The chapter’s structure is the structure of the gospel applied to daily life: the negative movement of putting off (vv. 5–11), and the positive movement of putting on (vv. 12–17). The things to be put off are the practices of the old self — sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, covetousness, anger, wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk, lying. The things to be put on are the character of the new self — compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forbearing one another, forgiving each other, and above all, love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.

The chapter then extends this transformation into the household (vv. 18–4:1): the practical ordering of the most intimate human relationships — wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters — under the lordship of Christ. These are not arbitrary social regulations; they are the gospel working its way into the fabric of daily life, the supremacy of Christ (chapter 1) arriving at the breakfast table, the bedroom, and the workplace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 3 turns from what the believer must not do (the rule-religion demolished in chapter 2) to a wholly new direction. “If then you have been raised with Christ” — and the “if” means “since”: the resurrection with Christ is an accomplished fact. The believer has already been raised, here and now — he need not climb a single rung through fasting, visions, or angels to reach the heavenly realm, for in Christ he is already there. From that ground come two commands that reach the whole inner person: seek the things above (the bent of desire and pursuit) and set the mind on them (the settled orientation of thought). This is no mystical escapism that despises the body, the job, or the home — it is the reordering of the entire life around the risen, reigning Christ, the way an exile lives and works in a foreign land with his heart fixed on home, for “our citizenship is in heaven.”

And the things above are not the celestial geography of the false teachers; they are wherever Christ is — “seated at the right hand of God,” the place of supreme honour and finished work, the very powers the Colossians feared now beneath his feet. The crucified one is the crowned one, and he reigns there as the believer’s own representative and advocate. Why seek what is above? Because that is where the believer’s true life now is: “you have died” (the old self buried with Christ) and “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — at once safe, locked in the most secure place in the universe, beyond the reach of any enemy, and hidden, not yet on display.

For the hiddenness has an appointed end. “When Christ who is your life appears” — he does not merely give life; he is our life — “then you also will appear with him in glory.” The ordinary, unremarkable believer, like an heir who has lived his whole life unrecognised, will be led out and revealed in glory beside the King on the day of his coming. That certain future is the great motive for present holiness, and it carries the whole section that follows.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer in Christ

Colossians 3:3 — “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — is one of the New Testament’s most comprehensive statements of the security of the believer. The life of the Christian is not exposed to the attacks of the world, the flesh, or the devil in any ultimate sense; it is hidden, concealed, kept safe in the most secure location possible: with Christ, in God. Reformed theology has always grounded assurance of salvation not in the believer’s performance but in the security of their position: in Christ, kept by God. This is why the Christian can face the world’s hostility and the flesh’s internal rebellion without ultimate despair; the life that matters is in a place nothing can reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that their spiritual security depended on correct navigation of the angelic hierarchy, proper observance of festivals and food laws, and achievement of special spiritual states. Paul says: your life is hidden with Christ in God. There is no spiritual power that can reach it; no ritual failure that can revoke it; no ignorance of esoteric knowledge that can diminish it. Now: The Christian whose sense of security rises and falls with their spiritual performance — who feels secure on days of devotional discipline and insecure on days of failure — needs to hear this: your life is hidden. It is not at risk. It is kept by the one whose power infinitely exceeds every force that would threaten it.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If then” — the turn of the argument. All through chapter 2 Paul has been pulling down the rule-bound, ascetic religion of the false teachers, ending with the verdict that such things are powerless to deal with sin (2:20–23). Now he gives the positive alternative. He has been working with two halves of one truth: in 2:20 he said, “if you died with Christ…why submit to regulations?” — the death-with-Christ that frees you from the world’s rules. Here he takes the other half: “if then you have been raised with Christ…seek the things above.” The point is decisive: the cure for a failed religion of rules is not no effort and no direction, but a new direction. Not down into severity to the body, but up toward the risen Christ. The Christian life is not asceticism; it is aspiration — the whole self reaching upward to where Christ is.

Does Paul mean “if” — or “since”? He means since. The little word (ei) here does not raise a doubt about whether the Colossians have really been raised with Christ; it reasons from the fact that they have. It is the same construction as 2:20. We could fairly translate, “Since you have indeed been raised with Christ…” Paul is not asking his readers to wonder whether they belong to Christ; he is building his command on the solid ground that they do.

“Raised with Christ” — pause and wonder. This is not a promise about the distant future; it is a statement about what has already happened. United to Christ (2:12), the believer shares his resurrection — now. The same almighty power that rolled the stone away and brought Jesus out of the tomb has raised Old Joe to new life. He is not waiting to be made alive someday; in Christ he is already as truly raised as his Lord is raised, because his Lord’s resurrection is his own. The grave is behind him; the new creation has already begun in him. And see how completely this answers the heresy: the false teachers urged the Colossians to climb — through fasting, through visions, through angels — to reach the heavenly realm. Paul says they need not climb a single rung. In Christ they have already been raised there. cf. Eph. 2:5–6.

“Seek the things that are above” — what does that mean? “Seek” (zēteite) is a present command — keep on seeking. To seek a thing is to pursue it, to set your desire and effort on it, to make it your aim and your treasure. And “the things above” are the realities of the realm where Christ reigns — his kingdom, his values, his priorities. But Old Joe may be puzzled, so let us say plainly what this does not mean. It does not mean floating about in mystical detachment, despising his job, his family, or his daily life — that would be the very escapism and asceticism Paul has just condemned. It is not a new set of rules, nor merely daydreaming about heaven. What it means is the reorientation of the whole bent of his life — his desires, aims, treasure, and ambition — around the risen Christ and his everlasting kingdom, rather than around the passing things of earth. The man who seeks the things above still drives his van and pays his bills; but he does it all for Christ and aimed at Christ’s kingdom, not as the be-all of his existence. It is a matter of what he is finally living for. “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. 6:21): to seek is to set the heart’s compass to point up.

“Where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” — why does Paul add this? He locates “the things above” with precision: they are where Christ is, and Christ is at God’s right hand. In the Bible the right hand of God is the place of supreme honour, of all authority and dominion, and of finished work — for Christ sat down there, his saving work complete (Ps. 110:1; Heb. 1:3; 10:12). Paul presses this for the comfort packed into it. The Christ Old Joe is told to seek is no dead teacher and no distant ideal; he is the living, enthroned Lord of the universe, seated at the centre of all power — and the very powers the false teachers feared lie beneath his feet (2:10, 15). And now let it land: the same Jesus who hung on the cross bearing Old Joe’s debt is now seated on the throne of heaven, ruling all things — the crucified one is the crowned one. The carpenter of Nazareth, the man of sorrows, sits at God’s right hand in glory; and he is yours, reigning there as your representative and your advocate (Rom. 8:34). To seek the things above is to seek him — and he could not be more secure, more powerful, or more entirely for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Set your minds on things that are above.” Verse 2 deepens verse 1. There Paul said “seek” (pursue, with desire and effort); here he says “set your minds” (phroneite) — another present, ongoing command. The word means more than passing thought; it is the settled bent of the mind, the whole orientation of one’s thinking, caring, and valuing (the same word as “have this mind among yourselves,” Phil. 2:5). What you habitually dwell on, ponder, and prize — set that on the things above, on the risen Christ and his kingdom. The seeking of verse 1 flows from a mind set there: aim the thoughts upward, and the life will follow.

“Not on things that are on earth.” And here is the deliberate counterweight. The mind is not to be set on “things on earth” — not the earthly, perishable things treated as ultimate: the possessions, status, and priorities of the old order (the perishable things of 2:22, and the very sins he is about to list in 3:5, which he calls “what is earthly in you”). The two cannot both be the mind’s true north at once. Whichever a man fixes his mind on will shape him: a mind set on earth makes an earthbound man; a mind set above makes a heavenly-hearted one. cf. Rom. 8:5–6; Phil. 3:19–20.

So that Old Joe understands it rightly. This is easy to take the wrong way, so let us be clear. “Set your mind on things above” does not mean Old Joe should become so heavenly-minded he is no earthly good; it does not mean despising the world, his body, his work, or honest pleasures (that is the asceticism Paul just demolished); and it does not mean drifting through life in a mystical haze. Of course Old Joe must still think about his job, his bills, and his garden — that is right and godly, and Paul will give him very down-to-earth instructions about home and work in just a few verses. The question is what his mind is finally set on: what he treasures, what governs him, what he interprets all of life by. Think of an Englishman living and working abroad: he does his job and pays his way in the foreign country, but his heart is set on home — his citizenship, his family, his future are there, and everything he does is coloured by where he truly belongs. So it is with the Christian: “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Old Joe lives and labours on earth with his heart set on home — on Christ, and the kingdom that will never perish. To fill the mind with Christ — his Word, his promises, his reign — and to view every earthly thing in that light: that is setting the mind on things above.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For” — the ground beneath the command. Why should Old Joe seek and set his mind on the things above? Paul gives the reason: “for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” The command rests on a fact about who he now is. His very life is located above, with Christ — so of course he should seek what is above, where his life actually is. And the two truths of the new self are now complete: he has been raised with Christ (v. 1), so he reaches upward; and he has died (v. 3), so the old earthbound life is behind him.

“You have died.” This is a finished fact (the tense points to a completed act): in union with Christ’s death, the old Old Joe — the self that belonged to the world and was ruled by its principles — has died and been buried with Christ (2:20; Rom. 6:2–6). That is why he no longer sets his mind on earthly things as his treasure: the man who lived for them is dead. His old identity is not merely improved or restrained; it is in the grave with Christ. A new self has been raised in its place.

“Your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Your true life — the real you, your new resurrection life in Christ — “is hidden” (a settled, permanent state), and the word carries two glorious senses at once. First, hidden means safe: your life is stored away, locked up, in the most secure place in all the universe — with Christ, who is himself in God. It is double-wrapped: your life in Christ, and Christ in God. No enemy, no power, no sin, no devil, not death itself can reach in and snatch it (John 10:28–29). Second, hidden means concealed: your true life and glory are not on display yet. The world cannot see it, and even you do not yet see it in full — for now it looks ordinary, unremarkable, often weak. But hidden is not lost; it is stored, waiting for the day it will be unveiled (v. 4).

This sounds lofty — but here is why Old Joe can rejoice. It may read like high mysticism, yet it is the most down-to-earth comfort a struggling believer could have. First, he is utterly secure. Old Joe’s real life — his salvation, his standing with God, his future, his very self — is not held in his own trembling hands; it is locked away with Christ in God, in the safest vault in existence. He cannot lose it. On his worst day, when he feels a failure and a fraud, his life is still safe, because it does not hang on his performance or his feelings but is hidden with Christ in God. Second, he is not yet what he will be. Right now Old Joe may look like nothing much — ordinary, aging, weary, unimpressive; the world sees no glory in him, and he may feel none. That is because his real life is hidden for now, like a seed buried in winter ground, like an acorn that does not yet look like the oak. But the glory is real, and it is coming: when Christ appears, what is hidden will burst into the open (v. 4). So Old Joe can lift his head. He does not have to achieve his life, guard it, or prove it; it is kept safe with Christ in God, and its hidden glory is on its way. cf. 1 John 3:2; Col. 2:3.

verseByVerse.quote: When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new note — and how it fits. Having spoken of present realities — you have been raised (v. 1), you have died, your life is hidden (v. 3) — Paul now lifts the eyes to the future, to the day of Christ’s return. This is the capstone of the whole paragraph and the answer to its deepest “why.” Why seek the things above and set the mind there? Because your life is hidden with Christ now (v. 3), and it will not stay hidden: when he appears, it will blaze into the open in glory. The pattern is hidden-now, revealed-then. And this verse is also the hinge of the letter’s argument: having settled who the believer is and will be (vv. 1–4), Paul is about to draw the practical conclusion — “Put to death therefore…” (v. 5). The future glory is the great motive for present holiness.

“Christ who is your life”. Notice the breathtaking phrase. Paul does not say Christ merely gives us life, as though life were a gift we then hold apart from him; he says Christ is our life — its source, its substance, its very centre. To have Christ is to have life; to be without him is to be without it. He is not an addition to Old Joe’s life, one good thing among many — he is Old Joe’s life. (This is the final answer to a heresy that offered Christ-plus: Christ is not part of the package; he is the whole of it.) cf. Gal. 2:20; Phil. 1:21; John 11:25.

“When Christ…appears”. The word means to be made manifest, brought out of hiding into open view. Right now Christ is hidden — enthroned at God’s right hand, unseen by the world. But a day is fixed when he will be revealed in glory and power before the whole creation, no longer veiled. And mark the word “when,” not “if”: his appearing is certain; only the hour is unknown.

“You also will appear with him in glory”. Here the believer’s destiny is bound fast to Christ’s. As his life is now hidden with Christ, so it will be revealed with Christ: when the Lord is unveiled, his people will be unveiled alongside him — and not in shame but “in glory.” The hidden life of v. 3 will be displayed at last, and Old Joe, who looks like nothing much now, will shine with the very glory of Christ, transformed into his likeness (1 John 3:2; Phil. 3:21; Rom. 8:17–18). The ordinary believer will be revealed in radiance beside the King of the universe.

This all sounds lofty — but here is Old Joe’s joy. Strip it down and it is the surest, most thrilling future a man could have. Right now Old Joe is hidden — plain, weary, unremarkable, often struggling, with nothing the world would call glorious about him. But a day is fixed when Christ will burst into view, and on that day Old Joe will burst into view with him, sharing his glory. What he truly is will finally be seen. Think of an heir to a great throne who has lived his whole life unrecognised, in working clothes, and the day of the coronation comes: he is led out, robed, and revealed before all as the king’s own son. That is Old Joe. He does not have to earn this glory, or guard it, or prove it — it is fixed and certain, because it is tied to Christ’s own appearing, which cannot fail. His story does not end in the grave or in obscurity; it ends in glory, with Christ. So he can carry the dullness and weakness of now with his head up: the best is not behind him and not even merely ahead of him — it is coming, and it is sure. cf. 1 John 3:2–3.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The imperative flows straight from the indicative: because you have died with Christ (v. 3), put to death what is earthly in you (v. 5). The word is violent — kill, execute — for sin is an enemy to be slain, not a pet to be tamed; yet this is no return to chapter 2’s flesh-punishing rules, which cannot touch the heart. It is mortification by the Spirit, from a standing already secured: become what you already are. The first list of sins runs from the outward deed inward to the desire — immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire — climaxing in covetousness, which Paul flatly names idolatry, the craving that sets created things where God alone belongs. Such sins are no trifles: the wrath of God is coming against them, and they were the very air the Colossians once breathed — though that life is now decisively past.

So Paul turns to a second image: “put them all away,” strip them off like filthy clothes — the anger that smoulders, the wrath that flares, the malice beneath both, the slander and the obscene talk that empty a corrupt heart through the mouth. And the deep ground of it all is stated twice: “you have put off the old self” and “have put on the new self.” The change of clothing has already happened, once for all, in Christ; the daily putting-off and putting-on simply live out an accomplished reality. Meanwhile that new self “is being renewed” — an ongoing work of God — “in knowledge after the image of its creator”: sanctification is nothing less than the restoration of the defaced image of God, the patient cleaning of a painted-over portrait until the likeness of Christ shines out again.

And this new self is corporate as well as personal. In it the great walls of the old humanity — race, religion, culture, class, down to the most despised Scythian — no longer divide; they are not erased as facts but dethroned. “Christ is all, and in all”: the one thing that finally defines a person is whether Christ is his, and the same indwelling Christ in every believer is what makes them one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification: Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s great treatise On the Mortification of Sin is the most sustained Reformed treatment of what Paul commands in Colossians 3:5. Owen’s central principle — “be killing sin, or it will be killing you” — reflects Paul’s logic exactly. The mortification Paul calls for is not the ascetic self-punishment that the Colossian false teachers practiced and Paul has just condemned (2:23); it is the Spirit-enabled application of the cross to specific sinful desires, the practical reckoning with what Christ accomplished: these desires belong to the old self that died in Christ; by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered an ascetic program that promised to deal with the flesh by external denial. Paul says: that program has no value in stopping the flesh’s indulgence (2:23). The real program is mortification — not external prohibition but the internal death-dealing of the Spirit to specific desires. The difference is not severity (asceticism can be more severe than mortification) but source: mortification flows from union with the crucified Christ. Now: The Christian who is fighting sin through willpower and self-discipline alone is using the wrong weapons. Mortification is spiritual warfare: the application of Christ’s death to specific sin patterns, in prayer, by the Spirit, in the community of faith. The fight is real; the weapon is the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put to death therefore” — the flow of the argument. The “therefore” reaches back to vv. 1–4. Because you have died and been raised with Christ, because your life is hidden with him and will appear with him in glory — therefore put the old sins to death. This is the great pattern of the Christian life: become what you are. You died to the old life as a finished fact (v. 3); now daily put to death its lingering expressions.
