And note the sharp contrast with chapter 2: this is not the asceticism Paul just condemned — rules and severity imposed from outside, which cannot touch the flesh (2:23) — but the killing of sin from the inside, by those already dead-and-raised with Christ.

“Put to death” — what, and how, for Old Joe. The word (nekroō) is violent: kill, execute, put to death. Not manage, not tame, not go easy on — kill. Sin is to be treated as an enemy to be executed, not a pet to be domesticated. What is to be killed? “What is earthly in you” — the sinful desires and habits of the old earthly nature that still cling to the believer (Paul lists them next). How? Here is the handle Old Joe needs. It is a paradox with v. 3: he has died with Christ once for all, yet he must put sin to death daily — the finished fact is exactly what fuels the ongoing fight. The killing is not done by the flesh-punishing rules of chapter 2; it is done “by the Spirit” (Rom. 8:13), in the strength of God, and from the standing of a man who already belongs to Christ. In practice that means Old Joe names the sin as the enemy it is, refuses it, starves it, flees the temptation, says a decisive and ruthless no — and does it leaning the whole way on the Spirit’s power, not gritting his teeth to earn God’s favour but fighting from a favour already his. “Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.”

“What is earthly in you”. Literally, “the members that are upon the earth” — the impulses and practices that belong to the earthly, fallen self. The link back to v. 2 is deliberate: these are the very “things on earth” the mind is not to be set on, now to be put to death. And note “in you” — the battlefield is inside, in the believer’s own remaining corruption. Then Paul names five, and the order is telling: he digs from the outward act down to the inward root.

The five named — from the deed to the desire. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for every sexual act outside marriage — fornication, adultery, prostitution, the lot (it gives us “pornography”); the outward deed. Impurity (akatharsia) moves inward — moral uncleanness, the defiled imagination and polluted inner life, not only the act but the filth behind it. Passion (pathos) goes deeper still — the ungoverned, driving lust that masters a person. Evil desire (epithymia kakē) reaches the very bottom — the wrong craving of the heart itself, the wanting that is set on what God forbids. Paul is exposing something vital here: sin is not merely bad behaviour to be tidied up on the surface; it runs all the way down into what the heart wants. That is why rules alone (chapter 2) can never cure it — they trim the deed and leave the desire alive.

“And covetousness, which is idolatry”. Paul crowns the list with a startling identification. Covetousness (pleonexia) is greed — the restless craving for more, the grasping after possessions, money, things that are not yours. And Paul calls it flatly what it is: idolatry. Why? Because to covet is to set the heart’s supreme desire and trust on something other than God — to look to created things for the security, satisfaction, and worth that God alone can give. Whatever a man treasures and trusts above God is his functional god; the greedy man bows at the altar of his own wallet (cf. Eph. 5:5; Matt. 6:24). This is why covetousness climaxes the list: it lays bare the idolatry beneath all these sins — every one of them is, at root, seeking in something other than God the life that only God can give. And it is the sneakiest of sins, for it wears a respectable coat: just “wanting a bit more,” just “a nicer life.” The cure is the same as the whole chapter’s: when Christ himself is your life (v. 4), the idols lose their grip. cf. Luke 12:15; Heb. 13:5.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of these the wrath of God is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The flow of the argument. Between the two lists of sins (v. 5 and v. 8) Paul pauses to give the reason they must be killed and stripped off: “On account of these the wrath of God is coming.” Why deal so ruthlessly with these sins? Because they are exactly what God’s judgment is set against. The wrath of God is the dark backdrop that makes putting sin to death not optional but urgent.

“The wrath of God is coming” — what does this mean? First, what God’s wrath is not: it is not a bad temper, a petty loss of control, or God flying off the handle. The wrath of God is the settled, holy, righteous opposition of a perfectly good God to all evil — his just and judicial reaction against sin. Far from a flaw, it is the necessary mark of his goodness: a judge who felt no opposition to injustice would be no good judge, and a God indifferent to evil would be no good God. Second, “is coming”: this wrath is real and on its way; a day of judgment is fixed (Rom. 2:5). These sins, then, are no trifles to be excused or kept as pets — they are the very things divine judgment is advancing against. For the believer there is deep sobriety here, and also deep relief: this is the very wrath that fell on Christ in his place (2:14), so that we are rescued from the wrath to come (1 Thess. 1:10) — which is all the more reason not to go back and dabble in what cost the Saviour so much. cf. Eph. 5:6; Rom. 1:18.

verseByVerse.quote: In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.
verseByVerse.commentary: “In these you too once walked” — is Paul saying every unbeliever does all these things? No — and the distinction matters. Paul is not claiming that every person outside Christ commits every sin on the list, or that all are equally vile in their conduct. People apart from Christ differ enormously; many are outwardly decent, kind, and restrained, for God’s common grace holds back the full flood of sin in the world. What Paul is saying is two things. First, this was the Colossians’ own former life: they “once walked” (it was their habitual road) in these very sins, “when you were living in them” (when such things were the element they lived and breathed in). Second, and more deeply, these sins are the native air of life apart from God — the realm the old life belongs to, its natural tendency and fruit, whether or not every sin shows its face in every person. The unredeemed heart is turned from God at the root (1:21), and this is the direction that turning runs. Notice the tender words “you too”: even you, now God’s holy people, were once in this. That is meant to do two things — to keep the believer humble (do not look down on those still trapped; you were there yourself) and to make him grateful (grace reached in and lifted you out). And it sets up the great pivot of v. 8: once you walked there — but now. That was your old country; you have emigrated; do not move back. cf. 1 Cor. 6:11; Titus 3:3–5.

verseByVerse.quote: But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now you must put them all away” — is this the same as “put to death,” and how is it done? “But now” is the great hinge from the old life to the new. The command “put away” (apotithēmi) shifts the picture: where v. 5 said kill (sin as an enemy to be executed), v. 8 says take off — like stripping off filthy, stinking clothes and throwing them aside. It is the same fundamental call to deal decisively with sin, under a new image: kill the root, strip off the garment. But how — for Old Joe, who has tried so often to “just stop” and still struggles? Here is the help. First, this is not mere willpower and white-knuckle suppression in his own strength; that is the chapter-2 asceticism that cannot conquer the flesh. Second, putting off always comes paired with putting on (v. 10, v. 12): you do not overcome a sin by leaving a hole where it was, but by replacing it — take off anger and put on compassion, take off lying and become a teller of truth. Sin is expelled not by a vacuum but by a stronger affection. Third, it flows from who he already is: he strips off these sins “seeing that he has already put off the old self” (v. 9) — he is not fighting to become someone new, but living out the new man he already is. And fourth, it is the work of a lifetime, done by the Spirit (Rom. 8:13) and carried along by God’s own renewing (v. 10). So Old Joe’s ongoing struggle is not proof that he has failed or that he is not truly Christ’s; it is the normal shape of the Christian fight. The old clothes feel familiar, and he keeps reaching for them — so he keeps taking them off again, day after day, leaning on the Spirit, and God keeps remaking him. Progress, not yet perfection. cf. Eph. 4:22–24; Heb. 12:1.

Anger, wrath, malice — the sins of the heart. Paul names three that lie close together but differ. Anger (orgē) is the settled, smouldering kind — the slow-burning resentment, the grudge nursed and harboured, the banked fire of ill-feeling that will not go out. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden kind — the flare-up, the outburst, the boiling-over of temper that explodes and (often) subsides: the blaze rather than the embers. Malice (kakia) is the root beneath both — the ill-will itself, the meanness of spirit that actually wishes another harm. Paul reaches past the hot words to the cold intent: the desire to see someone hurt. All three must come off.

Slander — and when is it slander, and when is it a fair warning? Slander (blasphēmia) is injurious speech against others — running a person down, tearing at his reputation, speaking evil of him. But Old Joe rightly asks: how do I tell slander from a legitimate warning? Scripture itself names real dangers and even real names (Paul warns of Hymenaeus, of Demas), so speaking of another’s fault is not always sin. The difference lies in three tests. Is it true? Slander traffics in falsehood, distortion, and the exaggeration that makes a tale juicier; a fair warning is accurate. Is it necessary, and for a good end? A warning aims to protect someone from real harm, or to help the person himself; slander serves only to wound, to entertain, or to make the speaker look better by comparison. And why am I really saying it — in love or in malice? A faithful warning is given reluctantly, in love, and usually to the person who can actually do something about it; slander is told with relish, behind the back, to anyone who will listen. So before Old Joe speaks of another’s fault, three questions: Is it true? Is it kind and necessary? And why am I saying it? If it is true, spoken in love, and needed to protect, that is warning. If it runs a man down for the pleasure of it, or to lift myself above him, that is slander.

Obscene talk — the sin of the mouth. Last comes “obscene talk from your mouth” (aischrologia) — foul, filthy, shameful speech: dirty language, coarse obscenity, the abusive and degrading word. Notice how Paul’s list has travelled — from the hidden heart (anger, wrath, malice) out to the open mouth (slander, obscene talk): the corruption within finally spills out in what we say. The tongue is the drain through which the heart empties (Matt. 12:34), which is why the new self must guard the mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not lie to one another”. One more sin of speech, given its own command: lying — and not only bald untruths but half-truths, spin, flattery, broken promises, the whole family of deceit. “To one another” presses it home: lying poisons the trust that holds the new community together, and so it is an assault on the very unity Paul is about to celebrate (v. 11). The new people of God are a people of truth, for their God is the God of truth and the devil is the father of lies (John 8:44); to deceive is to wear the old father’s likeness, not the new.

“You have put off the old self” — already done, or still to be done? And what is the “old self”? The verb is a completed past act: you have put it off — already, decisively, done. The “old self” (literally the “old man”) is not merely a bundle of bad habits; it is the whole person you used to be in Adam — your old identity and nature under the reign of sin, “with its practices,” the entire way of life that went with it. And Scripture says that old self was stripped off and crucified with Christ at your conversion (Rom. 6:6). So the foundational answer is: already done. The old man is not being slowly removed a piece at a time; he was taken off once for all in Christ. What remains — the daily putting-away of his leftover practices (vv. 5, 8) — is not the removal of the old self but the living-out of a removal already accomplished. That is the whole logic here: because the old self is already off, keep stripping off its rags.

“And have put on the new self” — already done, or still to be done? And what is it? Again a completed act: you have put on the new self. The “new self” (the “new man”) is the new person you now are in Christ — the regenerate self, the new creation (2 Cor. 5:17), your new identity in union with the risen Lord. It is also corporate: the new humanity Christ is forming, which is why v. 11 immediately says that in this new self the old divisions of race and class fall away. So both the putting-off and the putting-on are stated as done: in Christ, Old Joe has already taken off the old man and put on the new. His identity is settled. And yet — as the next words show — that new self, already put on, is not static.

“Which is being renewed” — the ongoing work. Here the tense changes: from the finished “put off / put on” to the continuous “is being renewed.” The new self, once and for all put on, is now in a process of constant renewal — made new, day by day. And it is passive: God is the one renewing it (cf. 2 Cor. 4:16; Rom. 12:2). So here is the answer to the puzzle of “already, or not yet?” — it is both. The decisive change is done (the old off, the new on: that is your settled identity); the transformation is ongoing (the new self being renewed: that is your daily growth). This is sanctification, and God himself is at work in it.

“In knowledge” — what is meant? The new self is being renewed “in knowledge” — and this is no dry collecting of facts, and certainly not the counterfeit secret “knowledge” the false teachers peddled. It is the true, deep, personal knowledge of God (epignōsis): coming to know him as he really is, in Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (2:3). The fall plunged the human mind into ignorance and darkness about God (Rom. 1:21; Eph. 4:18); the renewal reverses it — we come to know God truly again, and as we know him, we are remade. Knowing God rightly is itself transforming: you become like what you most truly know and behold.

“After the image of its creator”. The renewal is shaping the new self according to “the image of its creator” — and this reaches all the way back to the beginning. Man was made “in the image of God” (Gen. 1:26–27), and that image was defaced — though not erased — by the fall. Now, in Christ, God is restoring it: remaking the new self after the very image in which it was first created. And remember who the perfect image is — Christ himself, “the image of the invisible God” (1:15). So to be renewed after the image of the Creator is to be conformed to Christ (Rom. 8:29; 2 Cor. 3:18). Sanctification is nothing less than this: God re-stamping his own likeness on the human soul, restoring in you the image that was ruined in Eden.

So that Old Joe gets it — and takes heart. Put the whole picture together. Coming to Christ was like stripping off filthy, ragged old work clothes — the old self with all its sins — and putting on a clean new set — the new self in Christ. That change of clothes has already happened, once and for all: Old Joe is dressed in the new man. So the daily Christian life is simply this — live as the man you now are: keep taking off the scraps of the old filthy clothing you still find yourself reaching for (the sins of vv. 5 and 8), and keep wearing the new. And here is the heart of it for a struggler: while he does, God is at work on him like a master restorer cleaning a great portrait that has been painted over and grimed with age — patiently bringing back, stroke by stroke, the original image of the King that the fall had buried. Old Joe cannot always see the progress, and the cleaning can be slow; but the Master does not abandon a portrait he has begun to restore (Phil. 1:6). So when Old Joe still struggles, the answer is not despair but this twofold truth: the decisive change is done (you are the new man, clothed in Christ), and the renewal is under way (God is restoring his image in you). Keep putting off, keep putting on, and leave the renewing to the Restorer. cf. 2 Cor. 3:18; Rom. 8:29.

verseByVerse.quote: Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This looks like a new topic — but it is not. Paul has been speaking of putting off the old self and putting on the new (vv. 9–10); now he says that in this new self the old human divisions disappear. The link is the “new man.” The new self is not only personal but corporate — Christ is forming a whole new humanity, a new people — and in that new people the walls that divide the old humanity no longer stand. The renewal of God’s image in the individual (v. 10) goes hand in hand with the creation of one new people out of every kind of person.

“Not Greek and Jew…barbarian, Scythian, slave, free” — why list these? Paul names the great dividing-lines of his world, across every category. Greek and Jew — race and ethnicity, the deepest divide of all. Circumcised and uncircumcised — religion, the badge that marked the two apart. Barbarian, Scythian — culture: a “barbarian” was anyone whose speech sounded like babble to Greek ears, the uncivilized; and the Scythian was the byword for the lowest, wildest, most savage of all — Paul deliberately reaches to the most despised example imaginable. Slave, free — social class, the great fault-line of the Roman world. Race, religion, culture, class: Paul sweeps up the whole spectrum of human division, down to the most extreme, to make one point — in the new humanity, none of these any longer defines a person or divides the body. There is no one so foreign, so low, so looked-down-upon that he cannot be one in Christ with anyone else. The walls that structured the entire ancient world (and ours) come down at the foot of the cross. They are not erased as facts — a Jew is still a Jew, a slave still a slave — but they are dethroned: they no longer decide a person’s worth, his standing before God, or his place in the family.

“But Christ is all, and in all” — what Old Joe must grasp. Here is the glorious replacement for all those labels. “Christ is all” — he is everything, the sum and substance, the one thing that finally counts. In place of the old categories that ranked and divided people, there is now a single defining reality: Christ. And “in all” — the same Christ lives in every one of his people, Jew or Greek, slave or free, polished or rough. That indwelling is what makes them one. Three things for Old Joe to take home. First, his worth and identity are no longer measured by the things the world ranks people by — his nationality, his job, his class, his schooling, whether he is “somebody” or “nobody” in the world’s eyes. Christ is all; the only thing that ultimately defines him is that he belongs to Christ and Christ is in him. Second, this makes him truly one with every other believer, however different — richer or poorer, of another race or background; they share the one indwelling Christ, so they are family, and Old Joe must never let the world’s divisions divide the church. Third, here is the wonder: the same Christ in whom all the fullness of God dwells (1:19) lives in plain, ordinary Old Joe. He is not on the outside of the blessing looking in — Christ is in him. cf. Gal. 3:28; Eph. 2:14–16.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the old self is stripped off, the new self must be clothed: “put on.” And Paul roots the command in identity before he names a single virtue — “as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved.” These graces are not a program to earn God’s favour but the wardrobe that suits those who already have it; the beloved can afford to love. So the new self puts on compassion and kindness, true humility (not the self-hating or showy counterfeit of chapter 2) and meekness (strength under control, not weakness), and patience — worked out in the friction of real church life as bearing with one another’s faults and forgiving real wrongs. And the measure of forgiveness is staggering: “as the Lord has forgiven you” — freely, fully, before we ever asked. Over all these is drawn the one garment that holds the rest together: love, the bond of perfect harmony.

From character Paul moves to the community’s shared life, and three things govern it. The peace of Christ is to umpire the heart and the body, making the call when tensions pull the one body apart. The word of Christ is to dwell richly — a resident, not a guest — overflowing into the mutual ministry of teaching and admonishing one another in wisdom, and into psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs that lodge the truth in the heart. And the whole is summed up in the most sweeping statement of Christ’s lordship in the New Testament: “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.” There is no secular corner; the humblest task, done as Christ’s representative and for his honour, becomes worship. And threaded through the entire section — three times in three verses — runs its keynote: thankfulness. The community that puts on the new self is a peace-ruled, Word-saturated, singing, and above all thankful people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The list of virtues in Colossians 3:12–15 is nothing less than a portrait of Christ himself: compassionate, kind, humble, meek, patient, forgiving, loving, peaceful. Reformed theology understands sanctification as progressive conformity to the image of Christ (Rom 8:29); the virtues Paul commands here are the specific contours of that image. They are not generated by the believer through moral effort; they are produced by the Spirit as the fruit of genuine union with Christ (compare the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23). The community that puts on these virtues is the community that is becoming what it already is in Christ: holy and beloved.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian community, like every early Christian community, was a mixture of people from very different backgrounds — Jewish, Greek, slave, free — with very different habits of relating and conflicting. The virtues Paul commands were counter-cultural in every direction: humility was scorned by Graeco-Roman aristocratic culture; forgiveness was a novelty in a world organized around honour and revenge. Now: The church remains the most diverse social reality in the world, and the virtues Paul commands remain equally counter-cultural. The church that is genuinely putting on compassion, kindness, humility, and forbearance will look radically different from any other community the world contains, because these virtues are the character of the one who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put on” — and how? The clothing image continues. Having stripped off the old sins (vv. 8–9), the believer now puts on the new virtues — he gets dressed in the character of Christ. The Christian life is never merely stopping the bad; it is actively clothing yourself with the good. How is it done? Deliberately and daily, the way you put on clothes each morning — you choose to act in compassion, kindness, patience, even before the feeling arrives, and very often the feeling follows the action. It is done from your identity (the next words, “as God’s chosen ones”), as the new person you already are. And it is done by the Spirit, for these graces are the fruit he bears (Gal. 5:22–23) and the very likeness of Christ — to put them on is to “put on Christ” (Rom. 13:14). This is the opposite of chapter 2’s rule-keeping: not severity imposed from outside, but Christ’s own character grown from within.

“As God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved” — why does Paul start here? Before he names a single virtue, Paul names who they are — three words, and all three are God’s prior work on them. Chosen (eklektoi, the elect): God set his love on them and picked them out before they had done anything to deserve it (Eph. 1:4) — the very title once given to Israel, now worn by all who are in Christ. Holy: set apart as God’s own treasured people. Beloved: dearly loved by God, sharing the belovedness of his beloved Son (1:13). This is no accident of order. The identity comes before the commands, and the commands flow from it. Old Joe does not put on these graces in order to become chosen, holy, and loved; he puts them on because he already is. And that changes everything: a man secure in being chosen and loved can afford to pour himself out for others — he loves from a fullness, not to earn one. The beloved can afford to love.

“Compassionate hearts, kindness”. The first garments are tender ones. Compassionate hearts — literally a “heart of mercy,” a gut-level pity that is genuinely moved by another’s pain and stirred to help; not cold duty but felt tenderness, the inward parts wrung by someone’s need. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is that compassion turned into action — the gracious, generous disposition that actually does good to others, treats them gently, goes out of its way to help. Compassion feels; kindness acts. It is the very kindness of God himself, which leads us to repentance (Rom. 2:4).

“Humility” — and let us be clear what it is and is not. Strikingly, this is the very word the false teachers had twisted into ascetic show (2:18, 23); here is the real thing. True humility (tapeinophrosynē) is a right estimate of yourself before God — knowing you are a sinner saved by sheer grace, wholly dependent on him, and therefore not above anyone; it “counts others more significant than yourself” (Phil. 2:3) and stoops to serve, as Christ himself stooped (Phil. 2:5–8). But note what humility is not. It is not thinking you are worthless, or wallowing in self-hatred — that is just self-absorption with a long face. It is not the fishing-for-compliments false modesty of the heretics. And it is not spinelessness or being a doormat. Humility is not thinking less of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less — the self forgotten because the eyes are on God and on others.

“Meekness and patience”. Meekness (prautēs), too, is widely misunderstood, so hear what it is and is not. It is not weakness, timidity, or spinelessness — not the man who cannot stand up for anything. The Greeks used the word for a wild horse that had been broken and tamed: all its power still there, but now under control, harnessed, gentle to the hand. So meekness is strength under control — the gentleness of one who could retaliate but chooses not to, who does not insist on his rights or lash back. Jesus was “gentle and lowly” (Matt. 11:29) yet cleansed the temple; Moses was “very meek” yet led a nation. Patience (makrothymia) is literally being “long-tempered” — the opposite of short-tempered: slow to anger, able to endure provocation and difficult people without exploding or giving up. It is God’s own patience with us (Rom. 2:4) worn toward others.

“Bearing with one another”. Here the virtues meet real life in the church. To “bear with” is to put up with one another — to endure each other’s rough edges, quirks, and irritating ways without letting them rupture the fellowship. Old Joe knows the cases: the brother who talks far too long, the one whose opinions grate, the sister always late, the personality that rubs him entirely the wrong way. To bear with them is to make allowance, to overlook the irritation, to keep loving them as they are rather than freezing them out — the way a family puts up with one another’s annoying habits around the same breakfast table, because they are family. Every church needs this daily, for people are wearing, and love bears with them.

“Forgiving each other…as the Lord has forgiven you” — and must I wait until they ask? Bearing-with handles the small irritations; forgiveness handles the real wrongs — “if one has a complaint against another,” an actual grievance. Suppose a fellow believer truly wrongs Old Joe: gossips about him, cheats him, lets him down badly, wounds him with a cutting word. To forgive is to release the debt — to refuse the grudge and the revenge, and not let the injury harden into a wall — just as God cancelled Old Joe’s own vast debt (2:14). And the measure is staggering: “as the Lord has forgiven you” — freely, fully, at infinite cost, and before you ever asked, while you were still his enemy (Rom. 5:8–10). So must Old Joe forgive only when the other apologizes, or just like that? Both halves of the answer matter. The forgiving heart — the release of bitterness, the refusal of revenge, the readiness and longing to forgive — he must have always, at once, whether or not the other ever asks; that is how the Lord forgave him, taking the first step while he was still in the wrong (Mark 11:25; Luke 23:34). He is never to nurse a grudge until the offender grovels. The full reconciliation — the “I forgive you” spoken and received, the relationship restored — is completed when the other turns and repents (Luke 17:3); restoration, by its nature, takes two. So Old Joe forgives from the heart immediately, holding nothing back, and stands ready, even eager, to fold the other back into full fellowship the moment he turns.

“And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony”. Love is the crowning garment — “above all these,” the outer robe pulled on over the whole wardrobe of virtues. What is this love (agapē)? Not mainly a warm feeling, not romance, not merely liking someone — you can love, that is, seek the good of, a person you do not naturally like. It is a settled commitment of the will to seek another’s good and to give yourself for it, at cost, regardless of merit or return — the love that “so loved…that he gave,” the love mapped out in 1 Corinthians 13. So it is not soft sentiment and not mere permissiveness; it is self-giving action. And why “above all”? Because love is the bond — syndesmos, a ligament (the very picture of 2:19) — that ties all the other graces together and ties the whole body of believers together “in perfect harmony,” in mature completeness. Compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience: without love they fall apart and ring hollow (1 Cor. 13:1–3); with love drawn over them all, they are bound into one beautiful, whole, mature character. Love is the thread that holds the entire garment together. cf. Rom. 13:8–10; John 13:34–35.

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts” — what, and how? The “peace of Christ” is the peace he won and gives — the peace he made “by the blood of his cross” (1:20): first, peace with God, the war ended and the sinner reconciled; and out of that, the settled, untroubled calm he leaves with his people (“my peace I give to you,” John 14:27), and the peace that should reign between them. And the word “rule” (brabeuetō) is the umpire’s word — the referee who makes the call and settles the contest. So Paul says: let Christ’s peace be the umpire in your heart. When you are torn or anxious, when relationships are strained, when a decision pulls you two ways, let his peace make the call — refuse what shatters it, choose what preserves it. Do not let anger, fear, or self-will referee your heart; let the peace of Christ do it.

“To which indeed you were called in one body”. Two things. First, this peace is part of your calling — God did not call you to strife but to peace (1 Cor. 7:15); it is not optional but the very thing you were summoned to. Second, you were called “in one body” — into the one body of Christ, the church (recall v. 11, the one new humanity made of every kind of person). So this peace is not merely a private inner calm; it is the bond meant to govern the body’s life together. Old Joe is no lone Christian; he was called into a body, and the same peace that should umpire his heart is to keep the whole church one.

“And be thankful”. A short command, but no afterthought — it is the first of three calls to thanksgiving in three verses (vv. 15, 16, 17), for gratitude is the keynote of this whole section. And it belongs right here, beside peace, because the thankful heart is the peaceful heart. Gratitude crowds out the grumbling, discontent, and sense of grievance that breed strife and anxiety; the man counting his mercies has no room to nurse complaints (cf. Phil. 4:6–7). A thankful Christian is a contented, peaceable Christian, and a thankful church is a peaceful one.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The word of Christ” — what is it? The phrase is unique to this verse. It means the message that is Christ’s — the gospel of which he is the heart, the apostolic teaching about him and from him that the Colossians received (“the word of the truth, the gospel,” 1:5). It is not narrowly only the red-letter sayings of Jesus, but the whole word that proclaims him; and rightly applied it embraces all of Scripture, which everywhere testifies to Christ and comes from him. Note the pointed contrast: let Christ’s word fill you — not the “philosophy and empty deceit” and human traditions of the false teachers (2:8, 22).

“Dwell in you richly” — what and how? “Dwell” (enoikeitō) means to take up residence — to live in, to settle, to make a home — not to drop by as an occasional visitor. And “richly” (plousiōs) means abundantly, lavishly, in full and spacious measure. So the word of Christ is to be a resident, not a guest, and a richly-housed one — furnishing every room of the heart and of the church’s common life. How? By deep and regular intake — reading, hearing, pondering, memorizing — and by the two channels Paul names next: mutual teaching and corporate singing. This is, in fact, how all the putting-off and putting-on of the previous verses actually happens: the mind is renewed (v. 10) as the Word takes up rich residence within. Let it so fill the house that it shapes everything.

“Teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom”. The richly-dwelling Word overflows into a mutual ministry. Teaching (didaskontes) is the positive imparting of truth — helping one another understand and grow. Admonishing (nouthetountes) is the corrective side — warning, counseling, urging a brother away from wrong and toward right (the same word Paul used of his own ministry, 1:28). And mark “one another”: this is not the task of the official teachers alone but of every member — ordinary believers ministering the Word to each other. It is to be done “in all wisdom” — skillfully and fittingly, with discernment to know what word the moment needs and how to speak it. So Old Joe both receives this and gives it; the Word in him is meant to overflow to others.

“Singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness”. The third overflow of the indwelling Word is song. Paul names a rich variety — psalms (the inspired Old Testament songbook), hymns (songs of praise to God and Christ, perhaps like the great hymn of 1:15–20), and spiritual songs (Spirit-prompted song of every kind); we need not press rigid distinctions, for together they mean the full range of sung worship. And notice: singing is itself a way the Word “dwells richly” and a form of “teaching one another” (so the parallel in Eph. 5:19) — sung truth lodges in the heart and ministers to the whole congregation as nothing else does. It is to be done “with thankfulness in your hearts to God” — gratitude again, now lifted in praise. Worship is the Word set to music in a thankful heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Whatever you do, in word or deed”. This is the sweeping summary of the whole section, and one of the most comprehensive statements of Christ’s lordship in all of Scripture. “Whatever” — nothing is left out. “In word or deed” — everything you say and everything you do, the two halves that together cover the whole of life. Not merely the “religious” parts, but the entire ordinary round — work, family, meals, rest, the chat in the street. There is no secular corner walled off from Christ; the whole of Old Joe’s Monday belongs under this word.

“Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus”. To act “in someone’s name” is to act as his representative — on his behalf, under his authority, for his honour, in dependence on him, and in a way worthy of him. So to do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus is to live as his man in all things: to drive the van, pay the bill, speak the word, and do the task as Christ’s representative, for his glory, by his help, in a manner that would not shame his name. This both consecrates the ordinary (the humblest task becomes service of Christ) and constrains the sinful (you cannot do in his name what dishonours it). Here is the heart of the whole ethical section — not a fence of external rules, as the false teachers wanted (2:20–23), but the lordship of Christ reaching into every word and deed from the inside.

“Giving thanks to God the Father through him”. And the third call to thanksgiving in three verses closes the section: everything done in Jesus’ name is to be wrapped in gratitude to the Father. “Through him” — our thanks, like all our approach to God, comes to the Father through Christ, the one Mediator through whom our worship is welcome (the final quiet answer to the angel-mediators of chapter 2: no other channel is needed or allowed). So the new life in its daily round has two marks woven through all of it: it is lived in the name of the Lord Jesus, and it overflows in thanks to the Father through him. Lordship and gratitude — every word and deed turned into worship. cf. 1 Cor. 10:31; Eph. 5:20.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With the great doctrine of the new self in place (3:1–17), Paul brings the lordship of Christ home — quite literally — to the household, the ordinary roof under which most of life was lived. He does not tear down the structures of the ancient home; he fills them with a wholly new spirit. The drumbeat of the whole passage is one phrase repeated in varied form — “as is fitting in the Lord,” “fearing the Lord,” “as for the Lord and not for men,” “you also have a Master in heaven.” The risen Christ of chapter 1 is now the governing reality of the breakfast table, the nursery, and the workplace.

And Paul takes the relationships two by two, and — here is the quiet revolution — he addresses not only the subordinate but the one who holds the power, laying a costly command on the strong. Wives are to submit as is fitting in the Lord; husbands are given the harder word — to love sacrificially as Christ loved the church, and never to grow harsh or bitter. Children are to obey, a thing that pleases the Lord and bears the family likeness of the obedient Son who was himself subject at Nazareth; fathers are not to provoke and crush their children but to nurture them. Bondservants are to work heartily, with sincerity of heart, as for the Lord Christ himself — the lowliest labour rendered to the King of kings, and rewarded with an inheritance that no earthly slave could ever receive; and masters, who in that world owed their slaves nothing, are commanded to deal with them justly and fairly. In a culture where the authority of husband, father, and master was absolute, every one of these paired commands to love, nurture, and do justice was startlingly counter-cultural.

None of this is bare rule-keeping. It is the overflow of the gospel just announced: those who have died and been raised with Christ (3:1–3), who do everything “in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17), now let that new life reshape the most intimate relationships they have. And running underneath is a great leveller: the Lord “shows no partiality” (3:25), and even the master “has a Master in heaven” (4:1). At the foot of the cross the husband and wife, parent and child, slave and master kneel side by side as sinners saved by one grace, servants of one Lord. Paul does not, in a sentence, abolish the social order of the Roman world — but he plants within it a seed of love and equality-before-God that, properly cultivated, could never leave that order unchanged.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household: Sacred and Ordinary

The household code illustrates one of Reformed theology’s most important convictions: there is no sacred-secular divide. The lordship of Christ claimed in the great hymn of chapter 1 arrives in chapter 3 at the level of household management, parenting, and the workplace. Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is not abstract theology; it is the practical implication of “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). The Christian who is an excellent spouse, a patient parent, and an honest worker is doing theology in the most concrete possible form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Graeco-Roman household was organized around the absolute authority of the paterfamilias — husband, father, master. His authority was legally absolute. Paul does not abolish this structure but fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. The counterpart to every command of submission is a command of love and care that was genuinely counter-cultural. Now: The application of these principles in contemporary household and work relationships continues to produce the same counter-cultural witness: the Christian employee who works with integrity “as to the Lord” even when unsupervised; the Christian employer who treats workers with justice and fairness; the Christian parent who encourages rather than exasperates. Each is a small enactment of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Wives, submit to your husbands” — what does it mean? First, the setting: with v. 17 Paul has said that everything is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, and now he brings that lordship right into the home. The word “submit” (hypotassō) means to order or arrange oneself under — and the form Paul uses is reflexive and voluntary: the wife places herself under, freely. It is not something the husband seizes or imposes; it is her own glad, chosen deference to her husband’s God-given role of loving leadership in the marriage (the “headship” of Eph. 5:23). Notice too that it is “to your own husbands” — this is about one marriage, not women in general deferring to men in general. Positively, it is a disposition of respect, support, and trust: a wife coming alongside her husband as his partner, honouring and strengthening his leadership rather than competing with or undermining it, and — when a real decision must finally be made and they still differ — trusting his lead. Paul even frames it as a reflection of something beautiful: the church’s glad submission to Christ (Eph. 5:24).

And, just as importantly, what it does not mean. Six things must be cleared away, for the word is so often abused. (1) It does not mean the wife is inferior. She is fully equal in worth, dignity, and standing before God — equally made in his image, equally redeemed, a co-heir of the grace of life (1 Pet. 3:7; Gal. 3:28). Submission is a matter of role and order, never of value — just as the Son is fully equal to the Father in deity yet gladly does the Father’s will. (2) It does not mean slavish obedience. Tellingly, Paul tells children and slaves to “obey” (vv. 20, 22) but tells wives to “submit” — the gentler word; a wife is not her husband’s servant or child. (3) It does not mean silence or having no voice. She is a strong helper and counterpart (Gen. 2:18); she speaks, advises, and may freely disagree — godly women in Scripture did exactly that (think of Abigail). (4) It does not mean obeying into sin. Her submission is “in the Lord,” so it can never run against the Lord; if a husband demands what God forbids, she must “obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). (5) It is not a licence for harshness or abuse — the very next verse forbids the husband to be harsh, and a wife is nowhere commanded to submit to cruelty or danger; where there is abuse, the church must protect, not preach “submit.” (6) It is not earned by the husband’s worthiness, nor is it the submission of all women to all men. In short: a strong, godly, free woman gladly honouring her own husband’s leadership — never a crushed or silenced one.

Briefly, what does it look like? Most decisions in a healthy marriage are simply made together, by agreement and mutual counsel; headship and submission rarely have to “kick in.” But picture the genuine deadlock: husband and wife have prayed, talked it through, and weighed it honestly — a move, a major purchase, a direction for the family — and they still disagree, yet a decision must be made. There the wife trusts and supports her husband’s leading rather than insisting on her own way or making him pay for it. Day to day it looks like this: she speaks well of him and to him, backs and strengthens his leadership instead of undercutting it, and treats him with genuine respect (Eph. 5:33). It is the picture of a Sarah (1 Pet. 3:5–6) — a woman of strength who freely honours her husband, not a doormat who has lost her voice.

“As is fitting in the Lord” — the argument. Paul does not ground the wife’s submission in custom, culture, or social pressure — he grounds it “in the Lord.” “Fitting” (anēkō) means proper, becoming, suitable; this ordering is the fitting and beautiful thing — but fitting in the Lord, that is, within the life of those who belong to Christ and live under his lordship. This is the same lordship of v. 17 (“do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus”) now reaching into the marriage. So three things follow. First, it dignifies her submission: it is not capitulation to a husband’s superiority but an act of devotion to Christ — she does it for the Lord, as part of her own walk with him, “as to the Lord” (Eph. 5:22). Second, it roots the command in Christ, not in shifting cultural fashion — it stands because he is Lord, not because society once expected it. And third, it limits the command: because her submission is “in the Lord,” it can never be a submission that dishonours the Lord. The same phrase that asks it also guards it.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Husbands, love your wives” — what does it mean? The word is agapē — not first of all a romantic feeling or a warm glow, but the deliberate, self-giving love of the will that seeks the wife’s good (the same love crowned in 3:14). Paul states it briefly here; his parallel letter spells out the standard in full: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Eph. 5:25). That is the measure — nothing less than the sacrificial, self-emptying love of Christ for his people. So the husband’s headship of v. 18 is here defined, and it turns out to be headship-by-sacrifice, not headship-by-domination: he leads by giving himself away. And mark how counter-cultural this was. The household codes of the ancient world loaded the duties onto the lesser party and told the husband almost nothing; Paul turns and lays on the man the harder command — to love his wife as Christ loved the church. It is a love that is sacrificial (her good above his own comfort), constant (a settled commitment, not rising and falling with his feelings or her loveliness on a given day), and active — it “nourishes and cherishes” her as a man cares for his own body (Eph. 5:28–29).

Briefly, what does it look like? It looks like a husband who puts his wife’s good ahead of his own comfort — giving up the evening, the hobby, the preference, to help her or simply to be with her. It looks like cherishing and nourishing her: providing, protecting, noticing, listening, speaking tenderly, building her up rather than taking her for granted. It looks like serving her in the small, daily, unglamorous ways (the Lord himself knelt to wash feet), and bearing the load with her. It looks like a man who keeps loving her on the day she is hardest to love, because his love is a covenant, not a mood. In a word, it looks like Christ — a husband who would lay himself down for his wife.

“And do not be harsh with them” — the besetting sin to avoid. The word (pikrainō, from pikros, “bitter”) means “do not be embittered toward them,” do not grow harsh, sharp, or sour with your wife. Having commanded love, Paul at once names love’s opposite — and he names it because it is precisely the husband’s characteristic temptation. The very strength and authority of his position can curdle into domination; a man can let small resentments harden into a cold, bitter, critical spirit toward the one he should cherish most. The present tense warns against the slow settling-in of such a spirit: do not let bitterness take root and grow.

What it looks like — and the cure. Harshness wears familiar clothes: the cutting tone, the sarcasm, the constant criticism that is never satisfied, the contempt, the short temper, the silence used as a weapon, the “winning” of every argument by sheer sharpness. Often it is the strange sin of the man who is gentle and pleasant with everyone — colleagues, friends, strangers — and saves his harshness for his own wife. The cure is the very character Paul has just commanded: the compassion, kindness, meekness, and patience of 3:12, and the readiness to forgive rather than to nurse a grievance until it sours (3:13). Where love would cherish, harshness wounds; and a wife was never given to her husband to be a target for his bitterness, but to be loved as Christ loves. cf. Eph. 5:25–29; 1 Pet. 3:7.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Children, obey your parents” — and how this looks changes with the years. Notice first that Paul speaks directly to the children — they are real members of the church, able to hear God’s word and answer it. “Obey” (hypakouete) means to listen and to do — not merely to feel respect but actively to heed. And this looks different at different ages. For the young child, it is plain, glad, prompt obedience in the daily round — coming when called, doing the chore, going to bed, minding mum and dad; this is the very nursery of discipleship, where a little one first learns to submit to God by submitting to those God has set over him. For the older child and teenager, the relationship matures but the call remains: obedience now expressed as honour and trust — keeping the household’s rules, receiving correction and guidance without rebellion, trusting a parent’s wisdom even when it chafes. And for the grown child who has left home and formed his own household, the word shifts: the duty to obey belongs to the years under the parental roof, but the duty to honour never expires. “Honour your father and mother” (Eph. 6:2) is for life — the adult child no longer takes orders as a boy did, but he never stops respecting, listening to, caring for, and providing for his parents as they age (1 Tim. 5:4, 8). Obedience belongs to childhood; honour is lifelong.

One needful word on “in everything.” The sweep is wide — the whole ordinary life of the home — but it is not absolute, for all human authority is held under God’s. The parallel reads “obey your parents in the Lord” (Eph. 6:1). A child is never bound to obey a parent who commands him to sin against God, for then the higher authority must be obeyed (Acts 5:29). But that exception is rare; the plain meaning, for nearly every child on nearly every day, is simply this: obey, fully and gladly.

“For this pleases the Lord” — why does it delight him so? Above all, because in obeying, a child walks in the very footsteps of the Lord Jesus himself. For Christ is the great obedient Son: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38); “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29); he was “obedient to the point of death” (Phil. 2:8). And here is the wonder — the eternal Son, the One by whom all things were made, spent thirty years in a carpenter’s home and “was submissive” to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51). The Lord of glory obeyed his earthly parents in Nazareth. So when a child obeys, he is bearing the family likeness of the Son who delighted to obey his Father — and that is a thing of beauty to God. Two other reasons join it. The obedient home reflects God’s own good order, the design by which he made the world to run on glad, ordered love. And the child’s obedience to his parents is, underneath, obedience to God, who set parents over him; to honour the authority God established is to honour God. Let a child hear it plainly: when you obey, you genuinely bring joy to the heart of God — and you do it not to win his love, but as one who already belongs to the obedient Son. cf. Prov. 1:8–9; Luke 2:51–52.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Fathers, do not provoke your children” — what is being forbidden? The word (erethizete) means to irritate, exasperate, stir up to resentment. The parallel puts it sharply: “do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Eph. 6:4). So here, as with the husband and the master, the one who holds the power is the one given the restraining word: a father’s strength is to build his children up, never to crush them. Fathers exasperate their children in a hundred ways — by harshness and a never-satisfied criticism, by unfairness and favouritism, by punishing in temper, by impossible expectations, by domineering control, by hypocrisy (demanding what he will not do himself), and by cold neglect that withholds all warmth and praise. The good way is the opposite of every one of these: patient, warm, consistent nurture that disciplines and encourages, and that points the child to Christ. It is worth seeing how this looks across the years.

The young child. A father provokes a little one by impatience and a sharp tongue over ordinary childish failings — the spilled cup, the slowness, the mess — by anger out of all proportion, by rules that change with his mood, by promises lightly broken, by expecting a small child to behave like an adult. The good way is gentleness and patience: clear, consistent boundaries held with warmth, getting down to the child’s level, generous affection and praise, expectations fitted to his age, and promises kept. And when a young child is provoked, the discouragement shows plainly — in tears and flinching, in a new timidity or clinginess, in a once-bright spark gone anxious and withdrawn. A little heart bruises easily.

The school-age child. Here a father provokes by constant criticism of schoolwork and chores, by comparing the child to a sibling or a classmate, by praise that never comes, by mockery and sarcasm, by overreacting to mistakes, by shaming him in front of others, by demanding a perfection no child can reach. The good way is to encourage and to notice — specific praise for honest effort, real interest in the child’s world (his games, his friends, the things he is proud of), discipline that is fair and explained rather than arbitrary, patient instruction, time and attention freely given. The discouraged school-age child gives up trying (“why bother — I’ll never be good enough for him”), grows sullen, begins to lie to dodge the criticism, and quietly stops bringing his small joys to his father at all.

The teenager. A father provokes a teen by clamping down with a control that will not loosen as the child grows, by still treating him as a little boy, by extending no trust and no freedom, by endless lecturing, by belittling his opinions or his appearance, by “because I said so” where a reason was owed, by hypocrisy, and by refusing ever to listen. The good way is to let trust and responsibility grow together, to listen to and respect a developing mind, to reason rather than merely command, to choose the battles that matter and let the rest go, to keep the relationship warm, to model integrity and even to own his own faults — and above all to point the young person to Christ, not merely to enforce a rulebook. When a teen is provoked, the discouragement runs deep: it erupts as open rebellion and bitterness, or — just as dangerous — it sinks inward into withdrawal, secrecy, a shut door, a deadened and joyless compliance, the look of a young heart that has quietly given up on its father.

The grown child — and the Father behind all fathers. Even a grown child can be provoked: by a father who still dictates, who criticises his choices, his spouse, or his way of raising his own children, who withholds approval to the end. The good way now is to honour the child’s adulthood — to advise when asked, to bless rather than control — and the provoked adult child shows his discouragement by distance, avoidance, and a quiet, weary keeping away. Through every stage one pattern holds, and it is the gospel that sets it: the earthly father is to father as God fathers his own — “as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Ps. 103:13). God disciplines, but he never crushes; he is firm, yet tender; he is the Father from whom all fatherhood takes its name (Eph. 3:14–15). And the Christian father parents not to earn anything, but out of the fullness of a man who is himself a dearly loved child of that Father — passing on to his children the very grace he has received. cf. Eph. 6:4; Heb. 12:7–11.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What was a “bondservant”? The word is doulos, slave. Slavery ran right through the Roman world — perhaps a third of the empire — but it was not the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries. People became slaves by capture in war, by birth to a slave mother, or by selling themselves to escape debt and poverty. A slave was legally his master’s property, owing labour and obedience; yet many were educated — doctors, teachers, estate managers — could hold some money of their own, and could in time be freed by their master or buy their own freedom. So it was a harsh and varied institution, not a permanent doom. (Paul is not blessing the system; elsewhere he quietly undermines it — “if you can gain your freedom, do so,” 1 Cor. 7:21; and in Christ master and slave are brothers, Philemon. He is teaching believers how to live for Christ inside a system the gospel would in time dissolve.) The parallel to the modern employee is real but partial: like the worker today, the slave laboured under another’s authority and owed honest work — but unlike him, the slave was owned, unpaid, and often without choice or exit. So the how-to-work of these verses carries straight across to any job; the conditions do not.

“Obey in everything those who are your earthly masters” — the command. “In everything” means the full scope of the master’s lawful direction — the whole task, not just the pleasant parts, done thoroughly and without shirking (with the same unspoken limit that governs all such obedience: never into sin, for the Lord outranks every master). And mark the exact phrase: “earthly masters” is literally “masters according to the flesh.” In a single phrase Paul has already put the human master in his place — he is your master only on the earthly, passing level; you have another and greater Master above him.

“Not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers” — then and now. “Eye-service” (a word Paul seems to have coined) is work that only happens while the master’s eye is on you — busy when watched, idle when his back is turned. The “people-pleaser” works to impress the man, to win approval or dodge punishment, putting on a show. It is one of the oldest temptations of the workplace, and it has not aged a day: the employee who looks busy when the manager passes and slacks when he is gone, who games the metrics and polishes appearances for the review, who gives the minimum that will not get him caught. The gospel has no room for “as long as nobody is looking” — because Someone always is.

“But with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord” — the new motive. Against all that, an undivided, genuine heart — the same whether watched or not — and a reverent “fear of the Lord.” Here is the great turn, and it is exactly as it sounds: you work well not because the master deserves it, not because he happens to be watching, but because you stand in awe of the Lord who is always watching and whose will this is. Even a slave with a cruel and thankless master serves with all his heart — not for the master’s sake at all, but for the Lord’s. The audience of your work has changed: it is no longer the boss; it is God.

“Whatever you do, work heartily”. The Greek is vivid: work “from the soul” — put your whole self into it, with energy and goodwill, not grudgingly or by halves. And “whatever you do” spares nothing from this — the menial task, the unseen task, the dreary task: stack the shelf, sweep the floor, fill in the form — from the soul.

“As for the Lord and not for men” — the principle that changes everything. Here is why drudgery becomes worship. You are not, in the end, working for the man who signs your orders; you are working for the Lord. Christ is your true Master, and every task is handed, as it were, directly to him. The earthly master may be unworthy, ungrateful, even cruel — it does not finally matter, because he is not the one you are ultimately serving. Hand the swept floor to Jesus, and a mean master cannot rob it of its glory (cf. Eph. 6:7; Col. 3:17).

“Knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward”. Now feel the force of this. Under Roman law a slave could not inherit — inheritances went to sons and heirs, never to slaves. Yet Paul promises this slave the inheritance — the whole eternal estate of God’s people (1:12), “imperishable…kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet. 1:4). The man who owns nothing and can inherit nothing on earth is a full heir of God. And see how the argument presses the command: the slave may get no wage, no thanks, no advancement from his earthly master — but the Lord sees, and will repay, not with coins but with glory. So serve heartily, with your eyes lifted past the thankless present to the certain reward. (Note: the inheritance is not wages earned — you receive it as a son, by grace; the “reward” is God graciously crowning the very service his own grace enabled.)

“You are serving the Lord Christ” — in what way? This is the clincher. When the believing slave does his master’s bidding, he is in reality rendering that service to Christ — it is Christ who receives it, Christ who is truly being served. The lowliest labour, done in faith, rises to the King of kings as service offered to him (cf. Matt. 25:40). So the slave is not merely the slave of some human master; he is, in the deepest truth of it, a servant of the Lord Christ — and there is no higher title in all the universe.

“The wrongdoer will be paid back…and there is no partiality” — who is warned? The word can reach both ways, and is meant to. To the slave it is a warning: do not imagine your low place lets you get away with lazy, dishonest, or spiteful work — “my master mistreats me, so I will cheat him” — for God repays wrong even in a slave. To the master it is a threat (the very next verse, 4:1, turns to address him): the master who wrongs his servant will not escape. The hinge is the last phrase — “there is no partiality.” God plays no favourites; he weighs the deed, not the rank. The Judge is not impressed by a master’s wealth nor dismissive of a slave’s lowliness. So the powerless need not fear that the powerful will buy their way out: every wrong will be repaid, by the Lord himself, at his judgment, with perfect even-handedness. cf. Rom. 2:11; Acts 10:34.

Now bring it into Old Joe’s world — and behold the beauty of it. Old Joe is no slave, but he has a boss, a job, and a great heap of work that is repetitive, unseen, and rarely thanked. Watch what this passage does to his Monday. The cleaner mopping an empty corridor, the clerk filling the same forms, the carer washing a body no one else will touch — when it is done “for the Lord,” it is laid into the hands of the King who flung the stars into space and bled upon a cross. His foreman may never say thank you; the Lord is keeping account, and forgets nothing. No task is too small to be worship, no worker too low to be Christ’s honoured servant, no good hour ever truly unseen. And here is the wonder that should raise the hair on the back of the neck: the slave who owns nothing, who can inherit nothing, who is invisible to the great of this world — he is the servant of the Lord Christ and the heir of all things. The drudgery turns to glory; the overlooked man is the honoured one; the dreary shift becomes the very stuff of eternity. And Old Joe does none of this to earn Christ — he is already his, already an heir — but as a beloved son carrying his clumsy day’s work up to a Father who is delighted to receive it. Whatever you do, Old Joe — do it for him. cf. 1 Cor. 15:58.

4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview:
The final chapter of Colossians is shorter and more personal than the preceding chapters but carries the letter’s theology into two final areas: the Christian’s relationship to prayer and to the world (vv. 2–6), and the network of relationships through which the gospel advances (vv. 7–18). Together they show the gospel in its two directions: upward (prayer) and outward (mission), and the community of people in whom those directions are embodied.

The instructions on prayer and conduct (vv. 2–6) are brief but theologically dense. Prayer requires steadfastness and watchfulness — active, alert engagement rather than routine. Thanksgiving is its constant accompaniment. The prayer for open doors for the word of the mystery of Christ — the mystery Paul himself is imprisoned for proclaiming — is the prayer of a man for whom the gospel’s advance is more important than his own comfort or release. Conduct toward outsiders is to be “in wisdom,” making the best use of the time, with speech that is “gracious, seasoned with salt” — the attractive, preserving, flavour-giving quality that makes the gospel winsome as well as true.

The closing personal greetings reveal the extraordinary network of relationships through which the gospel was advancing in the first century: Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark (the John Mark of Acts 15, apparently reconciled with Paul), Justus, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Nympha and her house church, Archippus. These are not decorative biographical details; they are the human face of the gospel’s advance, the community of grace in its concrete, particular, named reality.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The instructions on prayer are brief but exact: continue steadfastly, keep alert, give thanks. The three qualities together describe a prayer life that is neither perfunctory (steadfast, not occasional) nor passive (alert, not sleepy) nor joyless (thankful, not merely dutiful). The specific prayer request Paul adds — for open doors for the word of the mystery of Christ — is remarkable for a man in prison: he is not asking for release but for continued opportunity to proclaim the message that put him there.

The instruction on conduct toward outsiders (v. 5) — walking in wisdom, making the best use of the time — reflects the eschatological urgency that runs through all of Paul’s letters: time is short, opportunity is limited, the gospel’s advance requires the community’s wise engagement with those outside it. The speech that is “gracious, seasoned with salt” (v. 6) describes the quality of Christian conversation: not bland and inoffensive (salt preserves and flavours), not harsh and alienating (seasoned, not overwhelming), but the kind of speech that creates appetite for the gospel rather than resistance to it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steadfast Engagement, Not Occasional Request

Paul’s instruction to “continue steadfastly in prayer” (proskartereite) reflects the Reformed conviction that prayer is not an emergency resort but the fundamental posture of the creature before the Creator. The same verb is used in Acts 1:14 of the disciples’ prayer in the upper room and in Acts 2:42 of the early church’s corporate life. Steadfast prayer is the mark of a community that has genuinely reckoned with its dependence on God and genuinely believes that prayer moves the hands that move the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul, in prison, could not personally open the doors for the gospel’s advance. He could pray — and he could enlist the Colossians to pray with him. The prayer for open doors is the prayer of the person who has surrendered control of the gospel’s advance to the one who actually controls it. Now: The church that wants to reach the lost but neglects corporate prayer has misunderstood the mechanism by which God works. Open doors are God’s to give; prayer is the community’s engagement with the God who gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Masters” — who were they, and what is the bridge to today? The word is kyrioi — the very same word as “Lord.” In the Roman world a master held near-absolute power over his slaves: he could command, punish, sell, and (in law) even kill them, with little or no accountability. A slave was reckoned property — Aristotle had called him “a living tool” — an economic asset valued for what he produced, not a person with rights. The duties of the household ran one way only, from slave up to master; almost no one thought a master owed his slaves anything. That is what makes this verse quietly revolutionary: Paul turns and addresses the masters, and lays an obligation on them. The bridge to our world is the employer — the boss, the manager, the business owner, the executive, anyone who holds power over other people’s work and livelihood. The old temptation survives intact: to see workers as “resources” (we even say human resources), units of production, replaceable cogs valued only for their output and the bottom line. To every Christian who holds such power, this verse speaks directly.

“Treat your bondservants justly and fairly”. Two words carry it. “Justly” (to dikaion) means to render what is right and due — honest dealing, what is owed, fair provision, discipline that is just and not cruel or arbitrary. “Fairly” (tēn isotēta) is literally equality, equity — even-handed, impartial treatment, with a hint of the deeper truth that in Christ this slave is in fact your equal and your brother. A standard like this went far beyond anything Roman law asked of a slaveowner: the one-way street becomes two-way, and the slave is suddenly a person to whom justice is owed. Picture it concretely — a Christian master in Colossae (think of Philemon) told to deal righteously with his slaves, even to welcome a runaway back as a “beloved brother” (Philem. 16). And bring it into the corporate world: the Christian employer owes his people a fair wage (not squeezing labour while profits soar), honest contracts kept, safe conditions, reasonable demands, no favouritism, no exploitation, no treating human beings as disposable. It looks like the owner who shares the gain fairly, the manager who disciplines by principle rather than by mood, the executive who will not cut the corner that harms his workers, the boss who treats the night cleaner and the senior partner with the same human dignity. The Christian in authority should be the most just and humane employer in town.

“Knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” — how the argument works. Here is the whole motive, and it is a master-stroke of wording: the master (kyrios) is told he has a Master (Kyrios). The man who holds the power is himself a servant; over the one who stands at the top of the earthly ladder stands One who owns him utterly. So Paul levels the hierarchy not by abolishing it but by pointing straight up: deal justly with those beneath you, because you will answer for it to the Lord above you — the same Lord who, he has just said, “shows no partiality” (3:25). The master’s wealth and rank buy him nothing at that throne; his Lord is watching how he treats the people in his power, and will repay. And there is a humbling sweetness folded in: master and slave have the same Master in heaven — they kneel side by side at one throne, equals before the God who made and bought them both. The cross levels everyone; at its foot the boss and the worker are two sinners saved by the same grace. The Christian who holds authority, then, wields it not as a little lord but as a fellow-servant who never forgets the Master over his own shoulder. cf. Eph. 6:9; Lev. 25:43; Job 31:13–15.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Continue steadfastly in prayer” — and notice that we are told to. The word (proskartereite) means to persevere, to hold fast, to stick doggedly at a thing and not give it up — the same word used of the first church, who “devoted themselves” to prayer (Acts 2:42). And the very fact that Paul must command it tells us something tender and true: staying steadfast in prayer is hard, and we need the encouragement. Why is it so hard? Because prayer is hidden, unseen labour with no visible machinery; because answers often tarry and we grow discouraged; because the flesh is weak and prayer can feel like “doing nothing”; because we are busy, distracted, and easily dried up; and because there is an enemy who would far rather we did anything than pray. So Paul does not say “pray when you feel like it” but “keep at it” — persevere. It was for exactly this that Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow, “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). Do not measure your praying by how it feels; simply do not stop. Every lapse is to be followed by a return; the goal is not perfect prayer but persistent prayer.

“Being watchful in it” — what did Paul mean? The word (grēgorountes) means to stay awake, alert, on guard — the picture is the sentry on night watch who dare not doze. It carries the memory of Gethsemane, where the Lord found his disciples asleep and said, “Watch and pray” (Matt. 26:41). To be watchful in prayer is, first, to pray awake — mind genuinely present, not a drowsy, mechanical mumble with a wandering heart. It is, second, to pray with open eyes — alert to what actually needs praying for (in your life, the church, the world) and expectant for God’s answer, like a watchman looking for the dawn. And it is, third, to be vigilant — for prayer’s great enemy is not so much hostility as drowsiness, the dull, half-asleep going-through-the-motions that empties prayer of life. Come awake, pay attention, mean it, and watch for God to act.

“With thanksgiving” — the indispensable companion. For the fifth time in this short letter, Paul sounds the note of thanks (1:12; 2:7; 3:15–17; here) — now woven right into prayer. Why does it matter so? Because thanksgiving keeps prayer from collapsing into a mere list of demands and complaints; it lifts the eyes from what we lack to all that God has already given. And that backward look fuels the perseverance Paul has just commanded — remembering yesterday’s mercies steadies the heart to keep asking today. The grateful pray-er is the persevering pray-er: thanksgiving crowds out the grumbling and discouragement that make us quietly give prayer up. And it is only fitting, for we come not to wring favours from a reluctant stranger but as children to a Father who has already given us his Son — so we ask with thanks already on our lips (cf. Phil. 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison — that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Pray also for us” — even Paul asked for prayer. Stop and feel the weight of this. Paul — the apostle chosen by the risen Christ, caught up to the third heaven, a writer of Scripture, the planter of churches across the empire — turns to a small congregation he has never even met and asks them to pray for him. The greatest Christian of the age leaning on the prayers of ordinary, faraway believers. The lesson is plain and humbling: even the best, the most gifted, the most mature of us never outgrows his need of God’s help and of his brothers’ prayers. If Paul needed praying for, how much more do we — and how much more should we pray for one another, for our pastors, our missionaries, our struggling friends. And it cuts the other way too: the humblest saint’s prayers truly count, for the prayers of this little church could shape the ministry of an apostle. Old Joe’s prayers for his pastor are no formality; they move the hand that moves the world. (Paul asks this everywhere — Rom. 15:30; Eph. 6:19; 1 Thess. 5:25.)

“That God may open to us a door for the word”. The “open door” is Paul’s picture for a God-given opportunity to preach (1 Cor. 16:9; 2 Cor. 2:12). And mark two things. First, it is God who opens it — the apostle can only walk through the doors the Lord swings open; even the chance to share Christ is a gift of God’s providence, not the fruit of our cleverness. Second, and tenderly: a man in chains does not ask for the prison door to open — he asks for a door for the word. His own freedom is not his concern; the gospel’s freedom is. “I am bound with chains,” he wrote, “but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). So pray for open doors — for gospel workers and for yourself — remembering that it is God who opens them.
